entries.русский: ввиду, учитывая; тж. букв. в виду, в пределах видимости
entries.register: formal in sense 1; neutral in sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause in sense 1 (in view of what happened last year). Never a that-clause — use in view of the fact that. Sense 2, the literal spatial one, takes a noun phrase only.
entries.pattern: In view of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] in view of [noun phrase]. · be in view of [noun phrase] (literal)
entries.contrast: Sense 1 is a formal because of and a close synonym of in light of and given; sense 2 is the literal, spatial reading. Do not confuse with in lieu of ("instead of") — the two are frequently swapped by writers who half-remember the phrase, and the resulting sentence means the opposite of what was intended.
entries.see also: in light of, because of, on account of, given, considering

entries.meaning: Alleges that the action broke a specific rule that governed it. Because the claim is legally loaded, careful writers use it only where the instrument can be identified and the breach is being asserted, not merely suspected.
examples: The fence was built in violation of the setback ordinance.
Three trades were made in violation of the firm's own policy.
The court held that the search was in violation of the Fourth Amendment.
Dumping in violation of the permit carries a fine for each day it continues.
She was dismissed in violation of the collective bargaining agreement.
In violation of the cease-fire, shelling resumed before dawn.
entries.русский: в нарушение (закона, правила) — утверждает нарушение конкретной нормы
entries.register: formal; legal, regulatory, and news writing
entries.complement: noun phrase — a statute, rule, order, permit, or agreement — or a free relative standing in for one (in violation of what the order plainly required). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] in violation of [noun phrase] · [noun] in violation of [noun phrase] · be in violation of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The negative counterpart of in accordance with and pursuant to: those report that the action followed the rule, this alleges that it broke one. The object must be an instrument that could be named and cited — which is why the phrase is so often followed by a section number — and that is what separates it from contrary to, which covers mere advice and expectations: you act contrary to advice, but in violation of a statute. Against plain against, it is the formal, citable form. Milder alternatives that stop short of alleging a breach are inconsistent with and at variance with.
entries.see also: in accordance with, pursuant to, contrary to, in keeping with, subject to

entries.meaning: States that the action conformed to a governing rule, standard, or instrument. It is the workhorse of compliance language and is almost never the right choice in ordinary prose, where under, following, or as required by will do.
examples: The audit was conducted in accordance with generally accepted standards.
Ballots will be counted in accordance with state law.
In accordance with your instructions, we have canceled the order.
The device must be installed in accordance with the manufacturer's specifications.
Benefits are calculated in accordance with the schedule in Appendix B.
entries.русский: в соответствии с — офиц.; согласно норме, стандарту или документу
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (in accordance with what the permit requires). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] in accordance with [noun phrase]. · In accordance with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: In accordance to is always an error — the noun accordance takes with. Against according to, which reports what a source says, in accordance with reports conformity to a rule: According to the manual, the valve closes (the manual says so) versus The valve was installed in accordance with the manual (the installation followed it).
entries.see also: according to, in keeping with, in line with, pursuant to, by virtue of

entries.meaning: Adds a second item to what the main clause already says. The added material is presented as supplementary, which is why it does not count toward the subject.
examples: In addition to the tuition, students pay a lab fee.
She speaks Portuguese in addition to Spanish and French.
In addition to running the shop, he teaches two nights a week.
The senator, in addition to three staffers, was subpoenaed.
In addition to being cheaper, the new part is easier to install.
The package includes breakfast in addition to airport transfers.
entries.русский: вдобавок к, помимо — добавляет второе, не делая подлежащее множественным
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (in addition to running the shop), or a nominal wh-clause (in addition to what the grant covers). Never a that-clause and — because this to is a preposition, not an infinitive marker — never a bare infinitive: in addition to run the shop is wrong, and in addition to running the shop is the only correct form.
entries.pattern: In addition to [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause]. · [clause] in addition to [noun phrase / verb-ing].
entries.contrast: Verb agreement trap. In addition to does not create a compound subject: The manager, in addition to two clerks, was present — singular, because only the manager is the subject. Coordinating and would make it were. The same rule governs as well as, along with, and together with. Against besides, this is the fuller, more formal version; against plus, the more written one. Bare in addition is a conjunctive adverb, not this preposition, and takes no object: The fee covers materials. In addition, there is a lab charge.
entries.see also: as well as, along with, together with, apart from, on top of

entries.meaning: Fixes the jurisdiction in which an official holds office and for whose benefit that office is exercised. It survives almost entirely on preprinted forms, and its stability there is exactly why it is worth recognizing.
examples: Sworn to before me, a Notary Public in and for the State of Ohio.
She was appointed a commissioner of deeds in and for the County of Kings.
The action was filed in the Superior Court in and for Maricopa County.
My commission as a notary in and for this state expires in March.
Grand jurors in and for the Eastern District returned a sealed indictment.
Outside the form book, in and for is simply for.
entries.pronunciation note: and reduces to /ən/ and for to /fər/, so the whole thing is in-un-fer · IN und FOR
entries.русский: в и для (округа) — юр., бланковая формула о юрисдикции должностного лица
entries.register: legal and official only; an American meets it on notary blocks, court captions, and commissions of office
entries.type: complex (two coordinated prepositions sharing a single object)
entries.complement: one noun phrase, naming a jurisdiction — a county, a state, a district. Never a that-clause, never a gerund, never a wh-clause. The two prepositions share the single object; there is no second slot.
entries.pattern: Notary Public in and for the [County / State] of [name] · [officer or body] in and for [jurisdiction]
entries.contrast: A frozen doublet of the kind legal English is full of — by and between, by and with, for and on behalf of, save and except — where two near-synonyms are yoked together for historical rather than semantic reasons. Nothing at all is lost by writing for: a notary public for Cook County says the same thing. Recognize it; do not imitate it outside the forms that print it. And note that it governs one object, so it is not the coordination of two separate phrases.
entries.see also: for and on behalf of, by or on behalf of, by and with the advice and consent of, by and through, save and except, in

examples: The festival is presented in association with the city arts commission.
The report was produced in association with two university laboratories.
The exhibit travels in association with the national gallery.
In association with the merger, four executives took early retirement.
Elevated readings were observed in association with long-term use.
The rash appears in association with the second dose, not the first.
Fatigue was reported in association with several of the older drugs.

senses.head: Jointly with; in partnership with
body: The festival is presented in association with the city arts commission.

senses.head: Occurring together with; correlated with (technical, and expressly not causal)
body: Elevated readings were observed in association with long-term use.
examples: The festival is presented in association with the city arts commission.
The report was produced in association with two university laboratories.
The exhibit travels in association with the national gallery.

Elevated readings were observed in association with long-term use.
The rash appears in association with the second dose, not the first.
Fatigue was reported in association with several of the older drugs.

entries.русский: совместно с, в партнёрстве с; тех. в сочетании с, коррелируя (не причинно)
entries.register: formal; institutional in sense 1, scientific in sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in association with [noun phrase] · [noun] in association with [noun phrase] · presented in association with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Two lives, and the register tells them apart. In credit lines and event billing it is a politer, looser in conjunction with: institutions co-present things in association with each other, where machines and medicines are used in conjunction with each other. In research writing it is a deliberately weak causal word — in association with claims co-occurrence and nothing more, which is exactly why journals prefer it to caused by or because of. A reader who treats sense 2 as a causal claim has misread it, and a writer who uses it hoping the reader will is being slippery.
entries.see also: in conjunction with, together with, along with, in accordance with, by means of

entries.meaning: Accuses two parties of secret cooperation toward a bad end. The tone ranges from a genuine allegation of corruption to affectionate teasing about a birthday surprise, and only context tells you which is meant.
examples: The inspector was in cahoots with the contractors he was supposed to be checking.
Half the county assumed the sheriff was in cahoots with the bootleggers.
My daughter is plainly in cahoots with her grandmother on this.
Two clerks in cahoots with an outside vendor moved four hundred thousand dollars.
He denied being in cahoots with anyone and produced the emails to prove it.
There is no in cahoot with: the noun is plural and always has been.
entries.русский: в сговоре с, заодно с — разг.; о тайном сообщничестве, часто шутливо
entries.register: informal; American colloquial and journalistic, and always disapproving or teasing
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun naming a partner in the scheme. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: be in cahoots with [noun phrase] · [clause] in cahoots with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Cahoots has no singular — nobody is in cahoot with anyone — and the noun appears in no other phrase at all, which is what makes this a frozen unit rather than a live one. Against in league with, which is the same accusation in a graver register, in cahoots with is folksy and often half-joking; against in collaboration with and in concert with, which are neutral, both of these presume wrongdoing. American in origin and still strongly American in flavor.
entries.see also: in league with, in conjunction with, at odds with, in collaboration with, on the side of

entries.meaning: Sets the main clause's subject beside a benchmark. Because it is bulky, it earns its place mainly when the benchmark is long or when the comparison needs to be fronted for emphasis.
examples: In comparison with last year, enrollment is up nine percent.
The salary looks generous in comparison with the regional average.
Our losses were trivial in comparison with theirs.
In comparison with the original, the remake feels weightless.
The drug performed well in comparison with the placebo.
entries.русский: по сравнению с — ставит подлежащее рядом с эталоном сравнения
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (in comparison with what we paid last year). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in comparison with [noun phrase]. · In comparison with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.variants: in comparison to is equally standard in American English; with is slightly preferred when the two things are being measured against each other, to when one is being likened to the other. Both are acceptable.
entries.contrast: A heavier compared with or than. Where a simple comparative will carry the sentence (This one is cheaper), the phrase is padding. Against relative to, which is neutral and quantitative, in comparison with is discursive. Bare in comparison is an adverbial, not this preposition: Last year was mild. This winter, in comparison, has been brutal.
entries.see also: relative to, as opposed to, in contrast to, contrary to

entries.meaning: States that the subject has met an obligation imposed on it. The phrase is evaluative in a way in accordance with is not: somebody was required to do this, and did.
examples: The facility is now in compliance with federal emissions limits.
All three buildings were brought in compliance with the fire code.
Records are retained in compliance with the state's retention schedule.
In compliance with the court's order, the agency released the remaining pages.
Contractors must certify that their subcontractors are in compliance with the wage rules.
The district reported that it was in compliance with what the settlement required.
entries.русский: во исполнение, в соответствии с — офиц.; обязанность была наложена и выполнена
entries.complement: noun phrase — a rule, order, permit, standard, or agreement — or a free relative standing in for one (in compliance with what the order required). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: be in compliance with [noun phrase] · [clause] in compliance with [noun phrase]. · In compliance with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.variants: In compliance to is an error — the noun compliance takes with, exactly as accordance does. The negative is out of compliance with, the standard regulatory phrasing for a lapse that is being corrected rather than prosecuted.
entries.contrast: Three phrases worth learning as a set: in compliance with reports that a duty was met, in accordance with reports that a procedure was followed, and in violation of alleges that a rule was broken. In compliance with presupposes an obligation the subject was under and usually implies that somebody checks, which is why it belongs to inspections, audits, and consent decrees rather than to ordinary description. Against under, which is shorter and better in ordinary prose, it earns its length only where compliance itself is the thing being asserted.
entries.see also: in accordance with, in violation of, pursuant to, in keeping with, subject to

entries.meaning: Marks joint operation or joint sponsorship. The two things named are doing something together, which is why the phrase is standard on instructions (use in conjunction with) and on event billing (presented in conjunction with).
examples: The exhibit was organized in conjunction with the state historical society.
This medication should not be taken in conjunction with alcohol.
In conjunction with the new sensors, the software can detect leaks earlier.
The training runs in conjunction with the annual conference.
Read this section in conjunction with the warranty terms on page 12.
entries.русский: совместно с, вместе с — о совместном действии или соорганизации
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in conjunction with [noun phrase]. · In conjunction with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Means "jointly with" or "used together with," not merely "and." Against along with and together with, which just add an item, in conjunction with asserts that the two things operate together as a unit. Against in association with, it is the more mechanical of the two: things are used in conjunction with each other, institutions do things in association with each other.
entries.see also: in association with, together with, along with, in accordance with, by means of

entries.meaning: Links the statement to a matter without specifying the link. Its usefulness and its emptiness come from the same source: it names a relation and declines to say which one.
examples: Two men were arrested in connection with the break-in.
She was questioned in connection with a series of unpaid invoices.
In connection with the merger, the company disclosed four side agreements.
Costs incurred in connection with the audit are reimbursable.
No charges have been filed in connection with what happened on the tenth.
entries.русский: в связи с — называет связь, намеренно не уточняя какую
entries.register: formal; legal, police, and corporate language
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (in connection with filing the claim), or a free relative (in connection with what happened on the tenth). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in connection with [noun phrase]. · In connection with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A deliberate vagueness word, and the vagueness is the point. Arrested in connection with the robbery reports that a person has been linked to it without saying how — which is exactly why police statements and news reports use it, and why an editor should leave it alone there and cut it everywhere else, where about, over, or for does the job in one word. Against in association with, which claims that two things co-occurred, in connection with claims only that something is relevant to a matter.
entries.see also: in relation to, in association with, with regard to, in respect of, in connection with

entries.meaning: Sets its object against the main clause as an opposite case. It signals the reader to expect difference, so the two halves must be genuinely comparable.
examples: In contrast to the coasts, the interior stayed dry all summer.
Her second novel, in contrast to the first, is almost cheerful.
In contrast to earlier models, this one runs silently.
The northern district gained population, in contrast to every other part of the state.
In contrast to what the ads suggest, the plan has a deductible.
entries.pronunciation note: in KAHN-trast too (noun stress on the first syllable; the verb contrast is /kənˈtræst/)
entries.русский: в отличие от — противопоставляет объект как противоположный случай
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (in contrast to what the ads suggest). Never a that-clause, and because the to is a preposition, never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: In contrast to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause], in contrast to [noun phrase].
entries.variants: in contrast with is equally standard. The bare adverbial in contrast (with no complement) is a conjunctive adverb, not a preposition: Sales fell. In contrast, margins improved.
entries.contrast: Against unlike, which is a single-word preposition doing the same job more economically, and against as opposed to, which adds a note of rejection or correction. Note that the complement must be grammatically parallel to what it is contrasted with, or you get a false comparison: In contrast to the 1990s, today's market is volatile compares a decade to a market.
entries.see also: as opposed to, contrary to, in comparison with, other than

entries.meaning: Names what is given back in a trade. Both halves of the exchange are stated, which is what distinguishes it from a simple for of price.
examples: He agreed to testify in exchange for immunity.
In exchange for the land, the developer will build a park.
She tutors his kids in exchange for studio space.
The company got tax breaks in exchange for keeping the plant open.
They released the documents in exchange for dropping the lawsuit.
entries.русский: в обмен на — называет то, что даётся взамен (не in exchange of)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in exchange for dropping the suit). Never a that-clause; a nominal wh-clause is possible but rare (in exchange for whatever they could salvage).
entries.pattern: [clause] in exchange for [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · In exchange for [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: In exchange of is an error — the noun exchange takes for, not of. Against in return for, which is nearly identical, in exchange for leans toward a transaction with two concrete sides, in return for toward a favor answered. Against plain for, both are explicit about reciprocity. Bare in exchange is an adverbial and takes no object: He gave up the patent and got nothing in exchange.
entries.see also: in return for, in lieu of, instead of, for

entries.meaning: Says the action fits the tone or precedent of what it follows. It is evaluative rather than regulatory, which is why it collocates with tradition, spirit, character, and wishes.
examples: In keeping with tradition, the outgoing chair gave the closing toast.
The renovation is in keeping with the character of the neighborhood.
In keeping with the family's wishes, the service was private.
His decision was entirely in keeping with everything he had said before.
The pay increase is in keeping with what other districts have offered.
entries.русский: в духе, в согласии с — соответствует традиции, тону, прецеденту
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (in keeping with what other districts have offered). Never a that-clause; a gerund is possible but awkward.
entries.pattern: [clause], in keeping with [noun phrase]. · In keeping with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Where in accordance with means conformity to a rule that binds, in keeping with means consistency with a spirit, tradition, or character — nobody is obliged. Compare in accordance with the statute (legally required) with in keeping with the family's wishes (fitting, not mandated). In line with sits between the two.
entries.see also: in line with, in accordance with, according to, contrary to

entries.meaning: Alleges a partnership, usually a secret or discreditable one. The metaphor is a formal treaty, which is why the accusation lands heavier than it does with the colloquial synonyms.
examples: The pamphlet accused the governor of being in league with the railroads.
Two of the guards were in league with the men who came over the wall.
She wrote as though the weather itself were in league with her enemies.
He was tried for being in league with a foreign power.
The smaller cities in league with Athens paid tribute every spring.
Nobody is in league with anybody here; it was a scheduling mistake.
entries.русский: в сговоре с, в союзе с — обычно о тайном и неблаговидном союзе
entries.register: neutral to formal, rhetorical; journalism, history, and polemic
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: be in league with [noun phrase] · [clause] in league with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Almost always pejorative, and that loading is what separates it from allied with and in alliance with, which are neutral. Against in cahoots with, it is the graver word: petty conspirators are in cahoots, but a government is in league with a hostile power and a villain is in league with the devil. The literal, unloaded use survives only in historical writing about actual leagues (the cities in league with Athens).
entries.see also: in cahoots with, in conjunction with, at odds with, in collaboration with, on the side of

entries.meaning: States that the subject is positioned to receive something by seniority, sequence, or expectation. American English uses line where British English uses queue, and both the literal and the figurative senses follow that split.
examples: She's in line for the deputy director's job when he retires.
Three of the plants are in line for upgrades next year.
As Senate president pro tempore, he is in line for the governorship.
Nobody had told him he was in line for a substantial raise.
We stood in line for forty minutes and never got in.
The team is in line for a top-five draft pick if the season ends today.
entries.русский: на очереди на, претендующий на — по старшинству, очерёдности или ожиданиям
entries.register: neutral; workplace, political, and sports reporting
entries.complement: noun phrase naming something expected to be received — a job, a promotion, a raise, an award, a draft pick. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: be in line for [noun phrase] · first/next in line for [noun phrase] · [person] in line for [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: In line for and in line with share three words and nothing else. In line for means "positioned to receive"; in line with means "consistent with." She is in line for the directorship is a prediction about her career; Her pay is in line with the market is a comparison — and swapping them produces nonsense. Against up for, which announces that a decision is coming and may go either way, in line for implies a queue in which the subject already holds a place. The literal use — standing in an actual line — is the ordinary American form where British English says in the queue for.
entries.see also: in line with, up for, in the market for, on the lookout for, on the verge of

entries.meaning: Reports that something matched an expectation, forecast, or policy. It is the standard verb-free way for analysts and reporters to say "as predicted."
examples: Third-quarter results came in in line with analysts' forecasts.
The proposal is broadly in line with what the committee recommended.
In line with company policy, all expenses over $50 require a receipt.
Wage growth is now roughly in line with inflation.
The new rules bring the state in line with federal standards.
entries.русский: в соответствии с, как и ожидалось — совпало с прогнозом или политикой
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (in line with what the committee recommended). Never a that-clause; a gerund is rare.
entries.pattern: [clause] in line with [noun phrase]. · In line with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Weaker than in accordance with (no obligation) and more quantitative than in keeping with — earnings come in in line with expectations. Do not confuse the frozen phrase with the literal in line with the doorframe, meaning physically aligned, which uses the same words and is also current.
entries.see also: in keeping with, in accordance with, according to, relative to

entries.meaning: Attaches the object of love — romantic or figurative — to the fixed predicate in love. The second sense is far commoner in written American English than the first, and it is nearly always faintly critical.
examples: She has been in love with him since their sophomore year.
They fell in love with the house before they read the inspection report.
The council is in love with the phrase "public–private partnership."
He is in love with the sound of his own voice and always has been.
I am not in love with the idea of driving nine hours in one day.
She's in love with hearing herself explain things to people who already know them.

senses.head: Feeling romantic love for
body: She has been in love with him since college.

senses.head: Infatuated with an idea, an object, or oneself — usually disparaging
body: The council is in love with the phrase "public–private partnership."
examples: She has been in love with him since their sophomore year.
They fell in love with the house before they read the inspection report.
The council is in love with the phrase "public–private partnership."
He is in love with the sound of his own voice and always has been.
I am not in love with the idea of driving nine hours in one day.
She's in love with hearing herself explain things to people who already know them.

entries.русский: влюблённый в; тж. неодобр. без ума от (идеи, себя) — второй смысл в письме чаще
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, and a gerund is fully idiomatic in sense 2 (in love with hearing herself talk). Never a that-clause. A free relative works in sense 2 (in love with whatever is newest).
entries.pattern: be/fall in love with [noun phrase / verb-ing] · madly/hopelessly in love with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The preposition is fixed: in love with, never in love to or in love of — and the plain verb love takes a direct object with no preposition at all, so She loves him, never She loves with him. Sense 2 is the one that earns its keep: He's in love with the sound of his own voice is an accusation of vanity that plain He loves his own voice does not deliver. Bare in love takes no object (They're in love), and fall in love is complete without with.
entries.see also: in awe of, in the mood for, fond of, crazy about, obsessed with

entries.meaning: States that one quantity varies with another at a steady rate. Because it makes a quantitative claim, it should not be reached for loosely where in line with is meant.
examples: Dues are set in proportion to each member's revenue.
Air resistance rises in proportion to the square of the speed.
The penalty should be in proportion to the harm actually done.
Seats are allocated in proportion to population, not land area.
Payouts are calculated in proportion to what each partner contributed.
Their share of the costs falls in proportion to the space they actually use.
entries.русский: пропорционально, соразмерно — количественная зависимость с постоянным коэффициентом
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative (in proportion to what each partner contributed). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: [clause] in proportion to [noun phrase]. · In proportion to [noun phrase], [clause]. · directly / inversely in proportion to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: In proportion with is an error — the noun proportion takes to. The negative counterpart is out of proportion to (a fine out of all proportion to the offense), which says the ratio is wrong rather than fixed.
entries.contrast: It asserts a ratio, which relative to and compared with do not: wages fell relative to rents says only that one moved against the other, while wages rose in proportion to hours worked says the two move together at a steady rate. Against sense 3 of according to (aid distributed according to need), the two overlap, but in proportion to commits to a measurable ratio where according to commits only to a criterion. The pair to know from science writing is directly in proportion to and inversely in proportion to.
entries.see also: relative to, in comparison with, in relation to, according to, in proportion to

examples: He was questioned in relation to a burglary in the same block.
The report makes no findings in relation to the second complaint.
In relation to staffing, nothing has been decided.
The fee is trivial in relation to the total cost of the project.
Their salaries have fallen sharply in relation to the cost of living.
The moon's size in relation to Earth is unusual among planets and satellites.

senses.head: Concerning; on the subject of
body: He was questioned in relation to the break-in.

senses.head: In proportion to; compared with
body: The fee is small in relation to the total cost.
examples: He was questioned in relation to a burglary in the same block.
The report makes no findings in relation to the second complaint.
In relation to staffing, nothing has been decided.
The fee is trivial in relation to the total cost of the project.
Their salaries have fallen sharply in relation to the cost of living.
The moon's size in relation to Earth is unusual among planets and satellites.

entries.русский: относительно, по поводу; тж. по сравнению с, в соотношении с
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (in relation to what was agreed in June). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: [clause] in relation to [noun phrase]. · In relation to [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Sense 1 overlaps with regard to and concerning; sense 2 overlaps relative to and compared with. The two readings can collide — small in relation to the budget is a comparison, questions in relation to the budget is a topic — and only the surrounding words disambiguate. Where sense 1 is meant, about or regarding is almost always tighter.
entries.see also: relative to, with regard to, with respect to, as to, regarding

entries.meaning: Marks the stimulus that the main clause answers. The relation is reactive rather than merely causal, which is why it is standard in official statements and in the methods sections of reports.
examples: In response to the complaints, the airline added two more flights.
Prices rose sharply in response to the supply disruption.
She wrote a four-page memo in response to a two-line email.
In response to your inquiry, the position has been filled.
The agency issued new guidance in response to the court's ruling.
entries.русский: в ответ на — стимул, на который действие является реакцией
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (in response to what the auditors found). Never a that-clause, and because this to is a preposition, never a bare infinitive — in response to receiving the notice, not in response to receive.
entries.pattern: In response to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] in response to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Causal like because of, but it requires that the object be something addressed to the subject — a question, a request, a crisis that demanded an answer. Because of the rain we canceled is a bare cause; in response to the rain would be odd unless the rain had made a demand. Bare in response is an adverbial with no object: They filed suit. In response, the city rewrote the ordinance.
entries.see also: as a result of, because of, owing to, further to

entries.meaning: Names what is given back as compensation or reciprocation. It presupposes that the first party gave something first.
examples: In return for her help, he fixed the transmission.
The union accepted a wage freeze in return for job guarantees.
She asks nothing in return for the work she does at the shelter.
In return for the endorsement, the campaign promised a speaking slot.
They got free housing in return for managing the property.
entries.русский: в ответ на, взамен — компенсация за то, что уже было дано
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause; a nominal wh-clause is possible but uncommon (in return for whatever help he could give).
entries.pattern: [clause] in return for [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · In return for [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with in exchange for in most sentences; in return for is the better fit when the second party is repaying a favor or a service rather than trading goods. The bare adverbial in return (no complement) is not a preposition: She helped him, and he said nothing in return.
entries.see also: in exchange for, in lieu of, thanks to, for

entries.meaning: States that the subject is a willing buyer for the thing named. Its negative is at least as common as its positive and usually means simply "not interested."
examples: We're in the market for a reliable used minivan, nothing fancy.
Are you still in the market for office space downtown?
The company is in the market for a chief financial officer with restructuring experience.
I am definitely not in the market for another opinion about my resume.
Buyers in the market for starter homes have almost nothing to look at.
He's been in the market for a decent used cello since September.
entries.русский: намеренный купить, подыскивающий — о готовом покупателе; чаще в отрицании
entries.register: informal to neutral; conversation, sales, and real estate
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a thing the subject would like to buy. Never a that-clause and never a gerund — in the market for buying a truck is wrong, because the object is the thing, not the buying.
entries.pattern: be in the market for [noun phrase] · not in the market for [noun phrase] (very common, and often ironic)
entries.contrast: The phrase is about wanting to buy, not about selling and not about the market as an institution. Against looking for, it specifies a purchase; against shopping for, it is less active and can describe mere willingness. Compare on the market, which describes the thing being sold (The house is on the market): the buyer is in the market, the goods are on it, and the two are not interchangeable. The negative has drifted into a general refusal formula with no money in it at all: I'm not in the market for advice.
entries.see also: in the mood for, on the lookout for, in line for, up for, in search of

entries.meaning: States a present inclination toward something. The entry earns its place mainly for the for/to split, which reproduces in miniature the central grammatical lesson of this whole file.
examples: I'm in the mood for Thai food and nothing else will do.
Nobody was in the mood for a two-hour meeting on a Friday afternoon.
Are you in the mood for a walk before it gets dark?
She was not in the mood for being told what her own data showed.
He's in the mood for an argument, so let's talk about it tomorrow.
Compare in the mood to argue, where to is an infinitive marker and takes a plain verb.
entries.русский: в настроении для, расположенный к — сиюминутная охота к чему-то
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in the mood for going out). Never a that-clause. Note the competing frame in the mood to + bare infinitive (in the mood to argue): that to is an infinitive marker, not a preposition, and it is one of the very few places in this file where a plain verb is correct.
entries.pattern: be in the mood for [noun phrase / verb-ing] · be in the mood to [plain verb] · not in the mood for [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: In the mood for takes a noun or an -ing form; in the mood to takes a plain verb. Both are correct English and they are not variants of one another: in the mood for arguing and in the mood to argue are the two available shapes, while in the mood for argue and in the mood to arguing are both wrong. Against feel like, which takes the same -ing complement, in the mood for is a shade more deliberate. The negative is commoner in practice than the positive and works as a soft refusal.
entries.see also: in the market for, up for, in love with, in need of, for

entries.meaning: States that a line of communication or of understanding is open between the subject and the object. The negative out of touch with does most of the phrase's rhetorical work and should be learned with it.
examples: I've been in touch with their lawyer twice this week.
Please put me in touch with whoever handles subrogation claims.
We've stayed in touch with the family since the trial ended.
She is remarkably in touch with what first-year students actually need.
The report says management is badly out of touch with conditions on the floor.
Six months in the hospital left him out of touch with everyone he used to work beside.

senses.head: In communication with
body: I've been in touch with their lawyer all week.

senses.head: Aware of and responsive to
body: She is remarkably in touch with what her students actually need.
examples: I've been in touch with their lawyer twice this week.
Please put me in touch with whoever handles subrogation claims.
We've stayed in touch with the family since the trial ended.
She is remarkably in touch with what first-year students actually need.
The report says management is badly out of touch with conditions on the floor.
Six months in the hospital left him out of touch with everyone he used to work beside.

entries.русский: на связи с; тж. чувствующий, понимающий (нужды, настроения) — ср. out of touch with
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, and a nominal wh-clause is fine (in touch with what her students actually need). Never a that-clause and never a gerund — in touch with feeling tired is wrong; in touch with how tired you are is a wh-clause and is right.
entries.pattern: be/get/stay/keep in touch with [noun phrase] · put [someone] in touch with [noun phrase] · out of touch with [noun phrase]
entries.variants: The negative counterpart is out of touch with, which takes the same complements and reverses both senses (out of touch with his own voters, out of touch with reality).
entries.contrast: Two senses that behave differently. Sense 1 is about communication and is neutral; sense 2 is about awareness and is nearly always evaluative — in touch with the mood of the country is praise, and out of touch with the mood of the country is the standard American insult for a politician. Bare in touch takes no object (Let's stay in touch), which is the commonest form of all. Against in contact with, sense 1 is warmer and less clinical, and in contact with is also the right phrase for physical touching, where in touch with is not.
entries.see also: in connection with, in relation to, in league with, familiar with, aware of

entries.meaning: Names the beneficiary of property held by someone else. The phrase encodes the central move of trust law — splitting legal title from benefit — and it does so on an ordinary bank form.
examples: The bank holds the certificate in trust for her two grandchildren.
The account is titled in his name in trust for his daughter.
Land was conveyed to the city in trust for the public as parkland.
Royalties are collected by the estate and held in trust for the surviving co-writers.
In trust for the benefit of the class, the settlement fund earns interest until distribution.
He is the trustee; the shares are in trust for the beneficiaries named in Schedule A.
entries.русский: в доверительном управлении в пользу — юр.; титул у одного, выгода у другого
entries.register: formal; banking, estate planning, and probate. An American meets it on a bank signature card — Mary Doe in trust for John Doe, abbreviated ITF — and in wills.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the beneficiary: a person, a class of persons, or a purpose. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: hold [property] in trust for [noun phrase] · [account] in trust for [noun phrase] · in trust for the benefit of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The complement of in trust for is the beneficiary, never the trustee — the trustee holds the shares in trust for the children — which is the reverse of what learners usually guess. Against in the custody of, whose complement is the keeper, this one names who the keeping is for. Against plain for, it adds that legal title sits with somebody other than the person who benefits, which is the whole idea of a trust compressed into three words.
entries.see also: in the custody of, for the use and benefit of, in behalf of, on behalf of, for the benefit of

entries.term: by and with the advice and consent of
entries.ipa: /baɪ ənd wɪð ði ədˈvaɪs ənd kənˈsɛnt əv/
entries.respell: weak /baɪ ən wəð ði ədˈvaɪs ən kənˈsɛn ə/
entries.meaning: Names the body whose concurrence makes an appointment or a treaty effective. The doubling of both the prepositions and the nouns is ceremonial; the operative content is "with the Senate's approval."
examples: The President shall appoint ambassadors by and with the advice and consent of the Senate.
Treaties are made by and with the advice and consent of two-thirds of the senators present.
His commission recites that he was appointed by and with the advice and consent of the Senate.
State constitutions copy the formula: the governor appoints by and with the advice and consent of the senate.
Modern drafters shorten it to with the advice and consent of, and then to subject to confirmation.
Nothing is lost when by and with the advice and consent of becomes with the approval of.
entries.pronunciation note: both ands reduce to /ən/ and the final t of consent drops before of · by und with thee ud-VYCE und kun-SENT uhv
entries.русский: по совету и с согласия — юр., церемониальная формула (об одобрении Сената)
entries.register: constitutional and official only; an American meets it in Article II of the Constitution, in the commissions issued to Senate-confirmed appointees, and in the state constitutions that copy the federal formula
entries.type: complex (a doubled doublet — two coordinated prepositions, two coordinated nouns, one object)
entries.complement: a single noun phrase naming the confirming body — in American practice, the Senate. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [nominate / appoint] by and with the advice and consent of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The source is Article II, Section 2: the President "shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint." Modern usage clips it in stages — with the advice and consent of, then with the consent of, then simply subject to Senate confirmation — and the full seven-word form now signals that you are quoting the Constitution or drafting a commission. Like for and on behalf of and in and for, it is a stacked legal doublet that adds no meaning the shorter form lacks; unlike by or on behalf of, it closes no real gap.
entries.see also: by leave of, by or on behalf of, for and on behalf of, in and for, under the authority of, by and through

entries.meaning: Attributes an achievement to sustained effort. It is a small, self-consciously literary preposition, and in modern American prose it is close to a set piece.
examples: By dint of sheer persistence, she finally got the records released.
He passed the bar by dint of six months of eighteen-hour days.
The team stayed in contention by dint of an absurd defensive record.
By dint of repetition, the phrase had lost all meaning.
She rose to partner by dint of out-working everyone around her.
entries.русский: благодаря, посредством — книжн.; об упорном, настойчивом усилии
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (by dint of working nights). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] by dint of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · By dint of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Means "by means of, through the force of," and is almost always followed by a noun of effort — hard work, sheer persistence, repetition. Against by virtue of, which cites a qualification or status, by dint of cites exertion. Dint is a fossilized word for "a blow, force" and appears in no other living phrase.
entries.see also: by virtue of, by means of, thanks to, through, by

entries.meaning: Names the authority whose permission made the act lawful or proper. Nearly every modern occurrence is the fixed phrase by leave of court.
examples: The amended complaint was filed by leave of court.
Additional discovery is permitted only by leave of the magistrate judge.
He addressed the chamber by leave of the presiding officer.
The society reprints the poem by leave of the author's estate.
By leave of the Crown, the company held the monopoly for twenty-one years.
The archaic By your leave survives as a stiff way of saying "excuse me."
entries.русский: с разрешения — юр.; почти всегда by leave of court «с разрешения суда»
entries.register: formal and old-fashioned; courts, legislatures, and ceremonial writing
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the granting authority — a court, a chair, a sovereign, an estate. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] by leave of [noun phrase] · by leave of court (article-less, fixed) · By your leave (a separate fixed formula)
entries.contrast: Leave here is the old noun meaning "permission," alive now only in this phrase, in on leave, sick leave, and the parting take leave. Against with the permission of, which is the plain modern equivalent, this sits a full register higher, and it is genuinely frozen in the legal collocation by leave of court — an amended complaint is filed by leave of court, never by permission of court. The fossil By your leave is a different and more archaic thing: it means "excuse me," and it takes a possessive rather than of.
entries.see also: by virtue of, by and with the advice and consent of, under the authority of, pursuant to, by order of

entries.meaning: Names the instrument or method that made the action possible. The plural means is invariable here; there is no by mean of.
examples: The sample is heated by means of an induction coil.
Access is controlled by means of a keycard system.
They crossed the ravine by means of a rope bridge.
The message was transmitted by means of a simple substitution cipher.
By means of a series of small loans, the cooperative rebuilt the mill.
entries.русский: посредством, при помощи — называет орудие или способ (не by mean of)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] by means of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · By means of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: An explicit by of instrument. Where plain by would be ambiguous between agent and instrument (The lock was opened by the technician versus by a magnet), by means of forces the instrument reading. In ordinary prose, by, with, or using is shorter and just as clear.
entries.see also: by way of, by dint of, by virtue of, by

entries.meaning: Covers both a party's own acts and the acts of anyone acting as that party's agent. It is one of the few legal doublets in this file that does real work, and the sentence around it usually shows why.
examples: Notice may be given by or on behalf of either party.
Any claim asserted by or on behalf of a shareholder is subject to arbitration.
Payments made by or on behalf of the borrower are applied in the order set out below.
Information collected by or on behalf of us is governed by this policy.
No statement made by or on behalf of the seller survives closing.
The distinction is real: by covers the party's own act, on behalf of covers its agent's.
entries.pronunciation note: or reduces to /ər/ and on to /ən/ · by or on bih-HAF uhv
entries.русский: самим или от имени — юр.; охватывает и свои действия, и действия представителя
entries.register: formal; contracts, notices, privacy policies, and arbitration clauses
entries.type: complex (two coordinated prepositional frames sharing one object)
entries.complement: a single noun phrase naming a party. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [act] by or on behalf of [noun phrase] · notice given by or on behalf of [party] · any claim brought by or on behalf of [party]
entries.contrast: This is a coverage formula, not a stylistic doublet, and that makes it the useful member of its family. It closes a gap either preposition alone would leave open: by the company covers the company's own act, on behalf of the company covers an agent's act, and drafters write both so that nobody can argue that a notice sent by outside counsel was not sent "by" the client. Against for and on behalf of, which is a signature-block formula and is genuine padding, by or on behalf of earns its length. Note the or: the two frames are alternatives, and one object serves them both.
entries.see also: on behalf of, in behalf of, for and on behalf of, in the name of, by and through

entries.meaning: Attributes a legal consequence to the fact that caused it. Its survival is purely professional: it says nothing because of does not say, and it says it two words longer.
examples: He was found not guilty by reason of insanity.
The lease may be terminated by reason of nonpayment.
No employee may be dismissed by reason of jury service.
By reason of their age, two of the defendants were tried separately.
The claim failed by reason of the plaintiff's own delay.
entries.русский: по причине, в силу — юр.; книжный двойник because of без прибавки смысла
entries.register: legal; largely confined to statutes, pleadings, and verdicts
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically an abstract one naming a condition or a failure (by reason of insanity, by reason of age, by reason of nonpayment). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause. A gerund is possible in drafting (by reason of having failed to appear) but the nominal is preferred.
entries.pattern: [clause] by reason of [noun phrase] · not guilty by reason of [noun phrase] (fixed) · By reason of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A legal because of, and outside legal writing that is what to use. Against by virtue of, which grounds an entitlement in a status the subject holds, by reason of names a cause of liability, exemption, or incapacity — which is why the two split so cleanly in practice: you chair the board by virtue of your office and are excused by reason of illness. The verdict formula not guilty by reason of insanity is fixed and admits no variation; by reason whereof is its archaic drafting relative.
entries.see also: by virtue of, because of, on the grounds of, pursuant to, by reason of

entries.meaning: Attaches a name to a person or thing already identified some other way. Outside fiction and police narrative it is nearly always a candidate for the blue pencil.
examples: A man by the name of Cross came to the door around eight.
She was traveling by the name of Ellen Weir.
He goes by the name of Sandy, though the paperwork says Alexander.
There is a village in Vermont by the name of Bread Loaf.
The report describes a suspect by the name of Ruiz, no first name given.
Editors will cut it: a man named Cross is shorter and says exactly as much.
entries.русский: по имени, по фамилии — присоединяет имя к уже как-то названному лицу
entries.register: neutral but faintly narrative or old-fashioned; storytelling, police reports, and dialogue
entries.complement: a name, and only a name — a proper noun or a noun phrase functioning as one (a man by the name of Fielding). Never a that-clause, never a gerund, and never a common noun: a dog by the name of a spaniel is nonsense.
entries.pattern: [a person] by the name of [Name] · go by the name of [Name]
entries.contrast: By the name of introduces the name; in the name of invokes an authority. A man by the name of Cross tells you what he is called; in the name of the people of this state tells you on whose authority you are acting. Against plain named and called, by the name of is longer and slightly literary, and editors cut it — a man named Cross says the same thing in two fewer words. The variant goes by the name of is the one that carries real information, since it implies an assumed or alternative name.
entries.see also: in the name of, as, in the person of, qua, in the capacity of

entries.meaning: Grounds an entitlement or a consequence in a qualifying fact. It is the standard formula for automatic, definitional consequences in legal writing.
examples: By virtue of her office, the mayor chairs the redevelopment board.
Children born here are citizens by virtue of the Fourteenth Amendment.
He inherited the title by virtue of being the eldest son.
The clause is void by virtue of the statute of frauds.
By virtue of its size alone, the company sets the market price.
entries.русский: в силу, на основании — основание автоматического, определяющего следствия
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (by virtue of being a resident). Never a that-clause; a nominal wh-clause is possible but rare (by virtue of what the charter grants him).
entries.pattern: [clause] by virtue of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · By virtue of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Cites a status, office, or inherent property as the reason something holds — by virtue of her office, by virtue of the contract. Against because of, it is narrower: the cause must be something the subject possesses or occupies. Against by dint of, which credits effort, this credits standing. Virtue here means "power, efficacy," not moral goodness.
entries.see also: by dint of, pursuant to, on the basis of, in the name of

entries.русский: через, транзитом через; в качестве, в виде (извинения); посредством
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] by way of [noun phrase / verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Three distinct senses, and they are told apart only by the complement: a place name gives sense 1, an abstract noun of function gives sense 2, an instrument gives sense 3. Against via, sense 1 is the plain-English equivalent. Sense 2 has no one-word substitute — by way of apology means "as an apology," and as alone would not carry the tentativeness.
entries.see also: by means of, through, by, as opposed to

entries.meaning: States the purpose behind an action that is only a first step toward it. It implies the goal is intended but not yet achieved, which is why it is so common in negotiation and planning language.
examples: The parties met with a view to settling the dispute.
The land was purchased with a view to future expansion.
They reorganized the department with a view to cutting overhead.
The bill was drafted with a view to surviving a court challenge.
She took the position with a view to eventually running the program.
entries.русский: с целью, в расчёте на — цель первого шага; далее -ing, не инфинитив
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund only. The to here is a preposition, not an infinitive marker, so with a view to increase costs is wrong — it must be with a view to increasing costs. This is the single most common error with the phrase. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] with a view to [verb-ing / noun phrase]
entries.variants: with a view toward and with an eye to are American alternatives; with a view to is the standard drafting form. British writers also use with a view towards.
entries.contrast: Means "with the aim of." Against in order to, which takes a bare infinitive (in order to reduce costs), with a view to takes a gerund (with a view to reducing costs). Mixing the two produces the classic error.
entries.see also: for the sake of, in search of, with respect to, to

entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (with reference to what you raised on Tuesday). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: With reference to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] with reference to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The letter-opening member of the with to group: sense 1 points back at a specific document or previous communication, where with regard to and with respect to point at a topic generally. Sense 2 is the technical one and is the reason the phrase survives at all — measured with reference to sea level means "using it as the baseline," which with regard to cannot mean. Note also with references to is an error in the topic sense, exactly parallel to with regards to.
entries.see also: with regard to, with respect to, further to, relative to, regarding

entries.meaning: Introduces the topic the statement is about. It is the formal register's about, and it is nearly always compressible — with regard to the budget is usually just on the budget or about the budget.
examples: With regard to the budget, no decision has been made.
The report says nothing with regard to enforcement.
With regard to your second question, the deadline has not changed.
Policies differ sharply with regard to part-time employees.
She has been careless with regard to deadlines all semester.
entries.русский: относительно, что касается — офиц. замена about; форма with regards to ошибочна
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (with regard to what the statute requires). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive: with regard to hiring, not with regard to hire.
entries.pattern: With regard to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] with regard to [noun phrase].
entries.variants: in regard to and as regards are equally standard; regarding is the one-word form.
entries.contrast: With regards to is an error. Regards with an s means greetings (give my regards to your mother), and it belongs at the bottom of a letter, not in the middle of a sentence. The singular regard is the noun meaning "attention, consideration." The same rule kills in regards to and as regards to. Note also that as regards takes no to at all.
entries.see also: with respect to, as regards, in relation to, as to, regarding

entries.русский: в отношении, касательно; мат. по (переменной): дифференцировать по времени
entries.register: formal; the standard American form in legal, technical, and academic prose
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (with respect to whether the filing was timely). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive: with respect to filing, not with respect to file.
entries.pattern: With respect to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] with respect to [noun phrase].
entries.variants: Abbreviated w.r.t. in mathematics and engineering. In respect of is the British counterpart; in respect to is a less common American variant.
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with with regard to as a topic marker, but with respect to also has a technical sense that with regard to lacks: differentiate with respect to x, symmetric with respect to the origin — "taking x as the variable or reference." Note that the phrase has nothing to do with deference; with all due respect is a different expression entirely. And as with with regard to, with respects to is an error — the plural belongs only in pay one's respects.
entries.see also: with regard to, in respect of, relative to, as to, in terms of

entries.meaning: Subtracts a named item from an otherwise universal claim. The claim must be a genuine generalization; subtracting from a specific statement produces nonsense.
examples: With the exception of Tuesday, the whole week is booked.
Every state, with the exception of Nebraska, has a bicameral legislature.
The building was undamaged, with the exception of two broken windows.
All fees are refundable with the exception of the application charge.
With the exception of one abstention, the vote was unanimous.
entries.русский: за исключением — вычитает пункт из утверждения об обо всех
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a gerund at a pinch (with the exception of having to repaint). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause — the clause-taking form is the conjunction except that.
entries.pattern: With the exception of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] with the exception of [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The heaviest member of the exception family. Except for, apart from, aside from, and bare except all do the same work in fewer words. It is worth the length only when the exception needs to be foregrounded, or in drafting where except alone might be read as attaching to the wrong element.
entries.see also: except for, apart from, aside from, save for, other than, excepting

entries.meaning: Names a contributor to an effort the subject remains responsible for. The main clause keeps the agency; the phrase only shares it.
examples: With the help of two neighbors, they had the roof patched by dark.
She finished the application with the help of a legal aid clinic.
The map was reconstructed with the help of nineteenth-century tax records.
With the help of a state grant, the library stayed open on Sundays.
He got through the first year with the help of whoever would tutor him for free.
entries.русский: с помощью — вклад помощника; ответственность остаётся за субъектом
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person, body, or instrument; a gerund is possible but uncommon. Never a that-clause. A free relative is fine (with the help of whoever happened to be around).
entries.pattern: [clause] with the help of [noun phrase]. · With the help of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.variants: with the aid of is the formal twin and is preferred for instruments (with the aid of a magnifying glass); with the assistance of is the most formal of the three; with help from is the looser conversational version. The of is not optional, and with the help from is an error.
entries.contrast: Against by means of, which names a pure instrument, with the help of usually names a collaborator and always implies that the subject did the work too — the helper assisted, and did not do it alone. That is also the difference from thanks to, which hands the credit over entirely: We finished thanks to Maria makes her contribution decisive, We finished with the help of Maria makes it partial.
entries.see also: by means of, thanks to, courtesy of, together with, with the aid of

entries.meaning: Quantifies the noun that follows. It is listed here because it wears the of costume of the complex prepositions and is frozen in exactly the same way — a lots of, a many of, and bare lot of are all impossible — while grammatically being a determiner, and because the subject–verb agreement it governs is the reason to learn it as a unit.
examples: A lot of the money set aside for repairs is still unspent.
A lot of people showed up who had never voted in a primary before.
There's plenty of time; the train doesn't leave until nine.
A number of residents are suing the county over the assessment.
The number of residents suing the county is now up to forty.
It took a bit of persuading and a couple of phone calls.
He talks a lot — and that bare a lot is an adverb, not this quantifier.
entries.pronunciation note: the t flaps and of reduces to a bare schwa, giving the ordinary spoken uh-LAH-duh · uh LOT uhv
entries.русский: много, масса — квантификатор при существительном; формально определитель, не предлог
entries.register: a lot of and lots of informal to neutral; a number of and a great deal of formal
entries.type: complex quantifier — a quantifying determinative rather than a true preposition
entries.complement: a noun phrase only. Never a that-clause, and no gerund as head (a lot of running is a noun). The real division inside the family is countability: a lot of, lots of, plenty of, a bunch of, and a ton of take either count plurals or mass nouns (a lot of chairs, a lot of furniture); a number of and a couple of take count plurals only (never a number of furniture); a bit of and a great deal of take mass nouns only (never a bit of chairs).
entries.pattern: a lot of [plural or mass noun] + [verb agreeing with that noun] · a number of [plural noun] + [plural verb] · the number of [plural noun] + [singular verb]
entries.variants: lots of, plenty of, a bunch of, a couple of, a number of, a bit of, a great deal of, a ton of — one frame, differing in register and in what each will count.
entries.contrast: The agreement trap is why this belongs in a book about frozen phrases. The verb agrees with the noun after of, never with lot or number: A lot of the money is missing but A lot of the files are missing. And in the number pair the article decides everything: A number of students are waiting (many students) versus The number of students is rising (one number). Against a true preposition such as out of, notice that the whole unit is the subject's determiner, not a modifier attached to it, which is why it governs no agreement of its own. Bare a lot is a degree adverb and takes no object — She travels a lot, Thanks a lot — and there it is not this item at all. Finally, a lot is two words; alot is not a word.
entries.see also: kind of, out of, in excess of, short of, a matter of, the better part of

entries.русский: за счёт (чьих-то средств); тж. ценой, в ущерб (чему-то)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (at the expense of losing accuracy). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] at the expense of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · [what was gained], at the expense of [what was given up]

entries.meaning: Names the agent responsible for harm, defeat, or mistreatment. The main clause supplies the injury and the phrase supplies who inflicted it, which is why it cannot be used where nothing bad occurred.
examples: The team suffered its worst loss of the season at the hands of an unranked opponent.
Hundreds died at the hands of the regime in the first month alone.
She described years of mistreatment at the hands of a former employer.
The manuscript met a sorry end at the hands of an overzealous editor.
The measure died at the hands of the very committee that drafted it.
He lost the title at the hands of a fighter nobody had heard of in March.
entries.pronunciation note: at reduces to /ət/ · at thuh HANDZ uhv
entries.русский: от рук (кого-то) — называет виновника вреда, поражения, дурного обращения
entries.register: formal to neutral; news writing, history, and sports reporting
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun naming a person, group, or institution — never an inanimate force. Never a that-clause, never a gerund. A free relative naming an agent is fine (at the hands of whoever was guarding him).
entries.pattern: [noun of harm or defeat] at the hands of [person or body] · [clause] at the hands of [person or body]
entries.contrast: An agentive phrase with a restriction built into it: what happens at somebody's hands is always something bad. A beating at the hands of the guards and a defeat at the hands of an unranked team are idiomatic; a gift at the hands of her uncle is not, and plain by is the neutral form for everything else. It also insists on a human or corporate agent, which is why damage at the hands of the storm is a misuse where damage from the storm is right — compare at the mercy of, which takes forces freely because it reports powerlessness rather than injury. Note that hands is invariable: there is no at the hand of in this sense.
entries.see also: at the mercy of, on the part of, courtesy of, because of, at the hands of, by

entries.meaning: Identifies the essential element of something larger. It is an argumentative move as much as a description: to put X at the heart of Y is to claim that everything else about Y is secondary.
examples: At the heart of the dispute is a single ambiguous sentence in the lease.
Water rights are at the heart of nearly every fight in the basin.
At the heart of the novel is a question the narrator never answers.
The audit found a filing error at the heart of the whole discrepancy.
At the heart of what the committee is fighting about is who signs the checks.
Trust, or its absence, sits at the heart of every one of these negotiations.
entries.pronunciation note: at reduces to /ət/ and the t of heart flaps into the of · at thuh HART uhv
entries.русский: в основе, в сердцевине — главное, по сравнению с чем остальное второстепенно
entries.register: neutral to formal; journalism, criticism, and argument
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (at the heart of deciding who pays), or a free relative (at the heart of what the committee is fighting about). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [noun] is at the heart of [noun phrase] · At the heart of [noun phrase] is [noun] (inverted, and very common)
entries.contrast: Figurative only: the literal anatomical string is in the heart, and at the heart of the chest is not English. Against in the middle of, which is spatial or temporal, at the heart of is about importance, not position — at the heart of the dispute names the essential issue, not the midpoint. Against at the center of, it claims essence where at the center of claims mere involvement: at the center of the scandal is usually a person, at the heart of the scandal is usually the issue. The inverted pattern, At the heart of the bill is a single sentence, is a stylistic staple and is worth learning as a unit.
entries.see also: in the middle of, in the midst of, on the basis of, in terms of, amid

entries.meaning: Places the subject under something it cannot control. What follows may be a person with power or a force with none — the phrase cares only that the subject cannot resist it.
examples: Small growers are at the mercy of whatever the wholesalers decide to pay.
The lifeboat was at the mercy of the current for nine hours.
Without the subsidy, the clinic is at the mercy of private donors.
The schedule leaves the whole project at the mercy of a single supplier.
Renters here are completely at the mercy of a market with no vacancies.
He refused to be at the mercy of a committee that met twice a year.
entries.pronunciation note: at reduces to /ət/ · at thuh MUR-see uhv
entries.русский: во власти, на милость — субъект не может этому противостоять
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person, body, or uncontrollable force. Never a that-clause, never a gerund. A free relative is fine and is common (at the mercy of whatever the wholesalers decide to pay).
entries.pattern: be at the mercy of [noun phrase] · leave someone at the mercy of [noun phrase] · entirely/completely/utterly at the mercy of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: It asserts powerlessness, not cruelty — at the mercy of the weather accuses the weather of nothing, and the phrase is fully idiomatic with forces that have no intentions at all. That is what separates it from at the hands of, which requires an agent and requires that harm actually occurred: you are at the mercy of a landlord before anything happens and at the hands of one only after it does. The related expressions have mercy on and without mercy are ordinary noun uses and not this preposition.
entries.see also: at the hands of, subject to, depending on, up against, in the face of

entries.meaning: Assigns a choice to a named party. In finance it is the phrase that tells you who holds the valuable side of an option, which is why it repays slow reading.
examples: The notes are redeemable at the option of the issuer after three years.
The lease may be extended for five years at the option of the tenant.
Payment is by check or wire transfer, at the option of the payer.
Arbitration is available at the option of the consumer only.
At the option of the buyer, the closing may be moved up by ten days.
Which party holds the option decides what it is worth, so read at the option of carefully.
entries.русский: по усмотрению, по выбору — юр.; кому принадлежит право выбора
entries.register: formal; contracts, bond indentures, insurance policies, and leases
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the party who holds the choice. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [right or action] at the option of [noun phrase] · exercisable at the option of [noun phrase] · at the option of the holder / the issuer / the buyer
entries.contrast: The complement is whoever gets to choose, not what is chosen — redeemable at the option of the issuer means the issuer decides, and for a bondholder that single phrase is the difference between a callable bond and a puttable one. Against at the pleasure of, which is about tenure in office and implies removal without cause, this one assigns a contractual election. Against plain if X chooses, it is the drafting form and is genuinely clearer in a document with several parties in play.
entries.see also: at the pleasure of, subject to, under the terms of, depending on, at the behest of

entries.meaning: States that a position is held only so long as the named authority wishes. It is one of the few phrases in American public life whose legal meaning is exactly its literal one.
examples: Cabinet secretaries serve at the pleasure of the president.
The city manager holds the post at the pleasure of the council.
Deputies are appointed by and serve at the pleasure of the sheriff.
She was reminded, not gently, that she served at the pleasure of the board.
Members of the commission serve fixed terms and are not removable at the pleasure of the governor.
Pleasure here means will, not enjoyment: the phrase is about who can fire you.
entries.русский: по усмотрению (назначившего) — должность держится, пока угодно этой власти
entries.register: formal; constitutional and employment law, and government service generally
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the appointing authority — a president, a governor, a board, a sheriff. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: serve at the pleasure of [noun phrase] · hold office at the pleasure of [noun phrase] · removable at the pleasure of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Pleasure here means will, not enjoyment, and the phrase is a statement about tenure: to serve at the pleasure of the president is to be removable at any time, for any reason or for none. That is the entire content of the expression, and it is why every American cabinet secretary is described this way. Against at the option of, which assigns a contractual choice, this one assigns the power to dismiss. Against at will, the employment-law term for the same arrangement between private parties, at the pleasure of is the public-office version. The British ancestor, during Her Majesty's pleasure, is a sentencing formula and means something else entirely.
entries.see also: at the option of, at the mercy of, under the authority of, subject to, at the behest of

He is a completely different person away from the office.
Away from the tourist streets, the city is quiet.
The nearest hospital is forty minutes away from the site.
We're one win away from the playoffs.
She has spent ten years moving away from what she was raised to believe.

senses.head: Separated from; not in the company of
body: He is different away from his family.

senses.head: At a stated distance or remove (with a measure phrase)
body: The school is two blocks away from here.
