entries.русский: прочь от, в сторону от; вдали от, вне (общества кого-то); на расстоянии от
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; never a gerund and never a that-clause. A free relative is fine (away from what she had grown up with). Sense 3 takes a measure phrase before it (two blocks away from).
entries.pattern: [clause] away from [noun phrase] · [measure] away from [noun phrase] · Away from [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Away alone is an adverb (She's away this week); the preposition needs from and an object. Against bare from, away from stresses separation and increasing distance rather than origin: He came from Detroit names a source, He moved away from Detroit describes a departure.
entries.see also: apart from, out of, close to, from

entries.meaning: Names the cause of the event in the main clause. It modifies the verb or the whole clause, which is exactly what distinguishes it from due to in the traditional rule.
examples: The flight was canceled because of fog.
Because of the strike, deliveries are running two days late.
She missed the deadline because of a family emergency.
He got the job because of who he knows, not what he knows.
Because of being out of the country, he never received the notice.
Attendance dropped because of the parking situation.
entries.русский: из-за, по причине — называет причину события (обстоятельство при глаголе)
entries.register: neutral — the default causal preposition of American English
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (because of being late), or a nominal wh-clause (because of who he knows, because of what the inspector found). Never a that-clause — because alone is the conjunction that takes a clause (because it rained), and because of it rained is impossible.
entries.pattern: [clause] because of [noun phrase]. · Because of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Because + clause versus because of + noun phrase is the cleanest preposition/conjunction pair in English: We stayed home because it rained / We stayed home because of the rain. Against due to, because of is adverbial and never disputed; against owing to and on account of, it is the plain, unmarked choice. The internet-era because noun (because science) is a deliberate joke and is not standard.
entries.see also: due to, owing to, on account of, as a result of, thanks to, in view of

examples: All photographs are courtesy of the state historical society.
The venue was donated courtesy of a local foundation.
Dinner is courtesy of the hotel, since they lost our reservation.
We got a flooded basement, courtesy of the city's storm drains.
Another three-hour delay, courtesy of the airline's scheduling.
He has a permanent limp, courtesy of one bad tackle in 1998.
The whole hallway smells like smoke, courtesy of whoever propped the fire door open.

senses.head: Given, lent, or supplied by (a credit line)
body: All images courtesy of the Newberry Library.

senses.head: As the result of (often unwelcome)
body: We got a flooded basement, courtesy of the city's storm drains.

entries.русский: любезно предоставлено (кем-то) — в титрах; тж. ирон. «благодаря» неприятной причине
entries.register: neutral in sense 1; informal and usually ironic in sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase, almost always naming a person, body, or organization; never a gerund and never a that-clause. A free relative naming an agent is idiomatic in sense 2 (courtesy of whoever left the gate open).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], courtesy of [noun phrase]. · [clause] courtesy of [noun phrase].
entries.variants: by courtesy of is the older full form and survives in formal credit lines; American English has generally dropped the by.
entries.contrast: Sense 1 is an attribution formula that presumes permission was granted — photograph courtesy of the state archive. Sense 2 has drifted into sarcasm and thanks nobody: a two-hour delay, courtesy of the airline. Against thanks to, which is also ironizable, courtesy of keeps a note of formal crediting even when the tone is bitter.
entries.see also: thanks to, on behalf of, by way of, because of

entries.meaning: Declares a complete absence of some quality. Because it is absolute, it resists hedging — somewhat devoid of is a solecism — but it takes intensifiers freely.
examples: The argument is utterly devoid of evidence.
His prose is elegant but entirely devoid of warmth.
The room was devoid of furniture except for a folding chair.
The claim is devoid of any legal merit.
She delivered the line devoid of inflection.
entries.русский: лишённый (качества) — книжн.; полное отсутствие, не допускает смягчения
entries.complement: noun phrase only, and characteristically an abstract mass noun (devoid of humor, devoid of merit). ✗ Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund. ✗ It cannot stand without of — there is no the room was devoid.
entries.pattern: be devoid of [noun phrase] · [noun] devoid of [noun phrase] · entirely/utterly/wholly devoid of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Stronger and more literary than without or lacking: devoid of asserts total absence, not mere shortage. Against void of, which is archaic outside legal boilerplate, devoid of is the living form. Against free of, which is positive (free of charge), devoid of is negative or critical.
entries.see also: void of, short of, in need of, exclusive of, in the absence of

entries.meaning: States non-identity between two things. It is freely gradable — slightly different from, no different from, completely different from — which is what keeps different a live adjective rather than a frozen particle.
examples: Her second album is completely different from the first.
Teaching adults is different from teaching eight-year-olds.
The rules are different from the ones we trained on.
The result was different from what anyone had predicted.
His account is not materially different from hers.
This model is no different from last year's except for the badge.
Nothing about the second inspection was different from the first.
entries.русский: отличный от, не такой как — нормативная американская форма (не different than)
entries.register: neutral — different from is the American standard
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (different from me, never different from I), gerund (different from working nights), or a free relative (different from what I expected). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [X] is different from [Y] · very / completely / no different from [noun phrase] · [noun] different from [noun phrase]
entries.variants: Different than is standard American English before a clause, where it saves a heavy from what: The result was different than I expected is accepted everywhere, and different from what I expected is the longer, unimpeachable form. Before a plain noun phrase — different than me, different than the others — it is the form editors change, and from is what to write. Different to is British and Australian and does not belong in American prose.
entries.contrast: The whole rule in one line: from before a noun, from what or than before a clause, never to in American writing. The reason from is the default is the verb behind the adjective — one thing differs from another, and nobody writes differs than. Against similar to, its exact opposite, the pair is worth memorizing together, because English hands the two comparison adjectives opposite prepositions and gives no reason for it. Against unlike, which is a one-word preposition doing the same job, different from is predicative where unlike is not: Unlike her sister, she plays cannot be rewritten as Different from her sister, she plays.
entries.see also: similar to, other than, as opposed to, in contrast to, different from, unlike

entries.meaning: Excludes an item from a stated total. It is a pricing and drafting word, and outside those contexts not including is better.
examples: The rate is $180 a night exclusive of tax and resort fees.
The team has eleven employees exclusive of contractors.
Damages are capped at $50,000 exclusive of interest and costs.
Delivery takes four business days exclusive of weekends.
The budget totals $2.1 million exclusive of capital expenditures.
entries.русский: не считая, без учёта — офиц.; исключает пункт из названной суммы
entries.complement: noun phrase only. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [statement of amount] exclusive of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The direct opposite of inclusive of, and the pair is the standard way to fix the boundaries of a quoted figure: $400 exclusive of tax versus $400 inclusive of tax. Against except for and apart from, this one is confined to quantities and lists — you cannot say exclusive of that, I enjoyed it.
entries.see also: inclusive of, with the exception of, except for, short of, devoid of

body: They live far from the nearest hospital.

senses.head: Not at all; the opposite of (with an adjective, noun, or gerund)
body: The building is far from finished.
examples: They live far from the nearest hospital.

entries.русский: далеко от (о расстоянии); тж. отнюдь не, вовсе не (far from finished — далеко не закончен)
entries.complement: noun phrase in sense 1; an adjective, a noun, or a gerund in sense 2 (far from perfect, far from a solution, far from being finished); a free relative in either (far from what we were promised). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] far from [noun phrase] · be far from [adjective / noun / verb-ing] · Far from [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause].
entries.contrast: Sense 2 is a negator, not a distance word. Far from perfect means "not perfect at all," and the fronted form — Far from helping, the new rule made things worse — denies the first idea and asserts its opposite, so a learner who reads it as a comparison gets the sentence exactly backwards. Against away from, which describes motion or growing separation, far from states a distance already in place: you move away from the coast and then live far from it. Bare far is an adverb and takes no object (We didn't go far, far too expensive), and the fixed reply far from it, meaning "not at all," takes the invariable pronoun and nothing else.
entries.see also: away from, close to, short of, other than, near

entries.русский: внутри (of необязательно); тж. амер. менее чем за (два часа)
entries.complement: noun phrase only. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund. Sense 2 requires a duration noun (inside of an hour).
entries.pattern: [clause] inside of [noun phrase] · inside of [duration]
entries.contrast: In the spatial sense the of is optional and usually edited out — inside the house is preferred to inside of the house in edited American prose, and British usage rejects the of outright. In the time sense, however, inside of an hour is an established American idiom that inside an hour only partly replaces, and within an hour is the neutral alternative. Bare inside with no object is an adverb: Let's go inside.
entries.see also: outside of, in the middle of, up to, in

entries.meaning: Replaces one option with another. Both options must be grammatically parallel — the commonest error is a mismatch, as in Instead of the bus, he walked, where a noun is being contrasted with a verb.
examples: Let's take the train instead of driving.
She ordered soup instead of the salad.
Instead of complaining, try filing a report.
He spent the afternoon reading instead of studying.
We met at the office instead of at the diner.
Instead of one long meeting, we'll have three short ones.
entries.русский: вместо — замена одного варианта другим; части должны быть грамматически параллельны
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (instead of driving), or a nominal wh-clause (instead of what you ordered). Never a bare infinitive — instead of to drive is wrong — and never a that-clause. Note that it does take a full prepositional phrase in the parallel-contrast pattern: We met at the office instead of at the diner.
entries.pattern: [clause] instead of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · Instead of [noun phrase / verb-ing], [clause].
entries.contrast: Instead of is the preposition and needs an object; bare instead is an adverb and takes none — We took the bus instead is correct, We took the bus instead of is not. Against in place of and in lieu of, it is the plain, unrestricted choice and the only one that takes a gerund comfortably in speech. Against rather than, which can join two verbs directly (rather than complain), instead of must nominalize (instead of complaining).
entries.see also: in place of, in lieu of, rather than, as opposed to, in favor of

entries.meaning: Dismisses a factor as irrelevant to what the main clause asserts. It is the drafting word for non-discrimination clauses and eligibility rules.
examples: The benefit is available to all employees irrespective of length of service.
Irrespective of cost, the repair has to be done this month.
Admission is open to applicants irrespective of nationality.
The rule applies irrespective of what the parties intended.
Irrespective of the outcome, the process was worth it.
entries.русский: независимо от, безотносительно к — офиц.; фактор объявляется несущественным
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (irrespective of what the survey shows). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] irrespective of [noun phrase / wh-clause]. · Irrespective of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Synonymous with regardless of, which is far more common in American English; irrespective of is the formal, legal-flavored twin. Note that irrespective is the correct word with the ir- prefix — the nonstandard irregardless is a blend of these two and should never be written.
entries.see also: regardless of, in spite of, notwithstanding, in the face of

entries.meaning: In its prepositional-looking use, kind of sorts a noun into a category, and the unit is frozen: no article inside it, and the number of kind decided by the demonstrative in front of it. The homophonous hedge is listed here only so you can tell the two apart, since it takes no object and is therefore not a member of this class.
examples: That kind of mistake is easy to make and very hard to undo.
These kinds of disputes usually settle on the courthouse steps.
It's a new type of battery, not simply a bigger one.
What sort of documentation does the office actually need?
He is not the kind of manager who tells you what he thinks.
Compare the hedge, which takes no object at all: I'm kind of tired.

senses.head: (classifier) A category or variety of
body: That kind of mistake is easy to make and hard to undo.

senses.head: (hedge, informal — takes no object, and so is not a preposition)
body: Somewhat, rather. I'm kind of tired.

entries.pronunciation note: reduced in speech to kinda, as sort of reduces to sorta · KYND uhv
entries.русский: род, разновидность (that kind of mistake); тж. разг. «вроде, как бы» — там не предлог
entries.register: neutral as a classifier; the hedging use is informal and belongs to speech
entries.type: complex classifier (kind, sort, type + of); the reduced degree adverb kinda is not a preposition at all
entries.complement: a bare noun, normally article-less (this kind of problem, that sort of thing, a new type of engine). Never a that-clause. A gerund is fine where it names an activity (the kind of thinking that gets people hurt).
entries.pattern: [this / that / what] kind of [bare noun] · [these / those] kinds of [plural noun] · a [adjective] kind of [noun]
entries.variants: sort of and type of work identically; sort of is the commoner British choice, kind of the commoner American one, and type of is the most technical of the three.
entries.contrast: Two different things wear these words, and only one of them takes an object. In that kind of mistake, kind of governs a noun and classifies it. In I'm kind of tired, it governs nothing — it is a degree adverb hedging an adjective, and by the test this file applies throughout (no complement, therefore no preposition) it falls outside the class entirely; the same goes for sort of in She sort of agreed. The number trap belongs to the classifier: make the demonstrative agree with kind, not with the noun — this kind of problem and these kinds of problems are both right, while these kind of problems is the classic nonstandard blend. And kind of a (that kind of a mistake) is dialectal in American English and gets edited out.
entries.see also: a lot of, in the form of, such as, a matter of, in the way of

entries.meaning: Gives the reason for the main clause. In edited American prose because of is the default and on account of is a stylistic choice; in speech it often signals a homelier register.
examples: The game was called on account of rain.
She retired early on account of her back.
On account of the holiday, the office closes at noon.
He was excused on account of being the only caregiver at home.
The road is closed on account of flooding.
entries.русский: из-за, по причине — стилистически проще и разговорнее, чем because of
entries.register: neutral to formal in standard use; the clause-taking version is regional and nonstandard
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (on account of being sick), or a nominal wh-clause (on account of what he said). A that-clause or a bare finite clause after it — on account of he was sick — is nonstandard in writing, though it is well attested in Southern and Appalachian speech and in dialogue.
entries.pattern: [clause] on account of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · On account of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A three-word because of, slightly more formal in writing and slightly folksier in speech, depending on the surrounding register. Against due to, it is safely adverbial. Note the unrelated literal phrase on account meaning "as partial payment" ($50 on account), which is accounting language, not this preposition.
entries.see also: because of, due to, owing to, thanks to, in view of

entries.meaning: Marks the person or body the speaker or actor is representing. It is the standard opening of formal remarks and the standard signature line of counsel and agents.
examples: On behalf of the entire staff, thank you for twenty years.
The attorney filed the motion on behalf of her client.
He accepted the award on behalf of his late father.
The union bargains on behalf of eleven thousand members.
On behalf of the mayor, I'd like to welcome you to the city.
entries.русский: от имени, по поручению — как представитель или агент кого-то
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, naming a person or body; never a gerund and never a that-clause. A free relative naming a person is fine (on behalf of whoever ends up holding the lease).
entries.pattern: [clause] on behalf of [noun phrase]. · On behalf of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.variants: in behalf of was traditionally distinguished in American usage — on behalf of = "as the agent of," in behalf of = "for the benefit of" — but the distinction has largely collapsed and on behalf of now covers both. In behalf of is safe to avoid.
entries.contrast: Against for, this specifies representation rather than mere benefit. Against in the name of, which invokes authority, on behalf of names a principal you are acting for. The reflexive form is on my own behalf, not on behalf of myself.
entries.see also: in the name of, in charge of, for the sake of, for

entries.meaning: Identifies what a decision, claim, or classification was grounded in. It is the standard formula in statutes, methods sections, and administrative findings.
examples: Applicants are ranked on the basis of test scores and interviews.
Discrimination on the basis of age is prohibited.
On the basis of the sample, the estimate is within two points.
The claim was denied on the basis of a paperwork error.
She was hired on the basis of what her references said, not her résumé.
entries.русский: на основании, исходя из — то, на чём построено решение или классификация
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (on the basis of what he saw). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the basis of [noun phrase]. · On the basis of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.variants: on the basis that is the clause-taking companion form and is a conjunction, not this preposition: on the basis that the contract had lapsed.
entries.contrast: Names the evidence or criterion a judgment rests on, where because of names a cause. Hired on the basis of her portfolio describes the grounds for a decision; hired because of her portfolio describes what made it happen. Non-discrimination law makes heavy use of on the basis of precisely because "grounds" is the legally relevant idea.
entries.see also: by virtue of, according to, in light of, pursuant to

entries.meaning: Names the stated reason for a decision, an objection, or a refusal. The reason is presented as one the speaker is prepared to defend, which is why the phrase belongs to rulings and appeals rather than to ordinary explanation.
examples: The application was refused on the grounds of cost.
Discrimination on the grounds of age is unlawful in every state.
He objected on the grounds of relevance.
She retired early on the grounds of ill health.
The documents were withheld on the grounds of national security.
The appeal succeeded on the grounds of what the trial transcript actually showed.
entries.русский: на основании, по мотиву — заявленное основание решения, возражения или отказа
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a recognized ground — age, race, national origin, cost, ill health, national security — or a free relative (on the grounds of what the inspector found). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the grounds of [noun phrase] · refuse / object / dismiss / discriminate on the grounds of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: on grounds of, without the article, is common in headlines and drafting; the singular on the ground of is older and now rare in American use. The clause-taking companion is on the grounds that + a full clause (on the grounds that the notice was late), which is a conjunction and not this preposition — the same split as in case of / in case and on the basis of / on the basis that.
entries.contrast: Exactly parallel to on the basis of, and the two are near-interchangeable in discrimination law, but on the grounds of leans toward a reason given for refusing, objecting, or excluding, while on the basis of leans toward a criterion used for deciding: you are hired on the basis of your record and dismissed on the grounds of misconduct. Against because of, this one claims the reason was formally stated, not merely operative.
entries.see also: on the basis of, because of, by virtue of, in view of, on the grounds of

entries.meaning: Marks an event as following hard upon another. The metaphor is pursuit, so the two events have to be close enough together for the second to be treading on the first.
examples: The layoffs came on the heels of a record quarter.
On the heels of the recall, two more suppliers suspended shipments.
The announcement arrived hard on the heels of the mayor's resignation.
A second storm followed on the heels of the first.
On the heels of losing the contract, the firm closed its Denver office.
The bill passed on the heels of three years of failed attempts.
entries.русский: сразу вслед за, по пятам — событие, наступившее вплотную за другим
entries.register: neutral to formal; a standard idiom of news writing
entries.complement: noun phrase naming an event; a gerund is possible but uncommon (on the heels of losing the contract). Never a that-clause. A free relative naming the event is fine (on the heels of what happened in March).
entries.pattern: come/follow/arrive on the heels of [noun phrase] · [clause], on the heels of [noun phrase] · hard/hot on the heels of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: hard on the heels of and hot on the heels of are the intensified forms and mean "immediately after." Heels is invariable — there is no on the heel of.
entries.contrast: Against in the wake of, the phrase it is most often confused with, this one claims closeness in time and nothing more: in the wake of the scandal says the scandal caused what followed, while on the heels of the scandal says only that the second thing came fast behind the first. Reach for in the wake of when you mean consequence and on the heels of when you mean the very next thing. Against plain after, both add speed and neither is neutral.
entries.see also: in the wake of, as a result of, subsequent to, in advance of, following

entries.meaning: States that the subject is watching for something while otherwise occupied. The noun lookout is a fossil of the naval watch, surviving in this phrase, in keep a lookout, and in the person posted as one.
examples: Be on the lookout for a silver pickup with a cracked windshield.
Nurses are on the lookout for early signs of infection.
She's always on the lookout for a first edition of that book.
Editors should be on the lookout for the same three errors in every draft.
Stay on the lookout for the turnoff; it isn't marked from this direction.
The bulletin asks agencies to be on the lookout for the vehicle.
entries.pronunciation note: on reduces to /ən/ · on thuh LOOK-owt for
entries.русский: высматривая, начеку насчёт — следит за чем-то, будучи занят другим
entries.register: informal to neutral; conversation, journalism, and police bulletins
entries.complement: noun phrase. Never a that-clause and never a gerund — on the lookout for hiring someone is wrong; write on the lookout for a new hire, or switch to looking to hire.
entries.pattern: be/keep/stay on the lookout for [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: This member of the on the frame closes with for, not of, and on the lookout of is simply an error. Against in search of, which implies active hunting, on the lookout for implies watchful readiness while doing something else. The object may be wanted (on the lookout for a bargain) or unwanted (on the lookout for signs of infection), which is where it parts from in the market for, whose object is always wanted. Bare on the lookout takes no object (Stay on the lookout).
entries.see also: in search of, in the market for, in line for, on the verge of, for

entries.meaning: Assigns an abstract behavior to the person or body responsible for it. It exists because English nominalizations drop their subjects, and this is the phrase that puts one back.
examples: There was no bad faith on the part of either side.
The report found negligence on the part of two supervisors.
Some reluctance on the part of the family is understandable.
It was a genuine misunderstanding on the part of the clerk.
Any failure on the part of the tenant to give notice voids the clause.
The delay reflects real indecision on the part of the board.
entries.русский: со стороны (кого-то) — приписывает отвлечённое поведение ответственному лицу
entries.register: formal; legal, academic, and report writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun naming a person or a body — never a thing. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [noun of conduct or attitude] on the part of [person or body] · There was no [noun] on the part of [person].
entries.contrast: Its one job is to attach an actor to an abstract noun of behavior — negligence, reluctance, failure, bad faith, misunderstanding — where the nominalization has lost the subject a verb would have carried: negligence on the part of the contractor is the contractor was negligent, kept nominal. That is also its weakness, since nine times in ten a by phrase or a plain verb is shorter. The complement must be animate — a failure on the part of the software is a misuse for a failure of the software. Do not confuse it with for my part ("as far as I'm concerned") or take the part of ("side with"), which are separate fixed phrases.
entries.see also: on behalf of, in the name of, by virtue of, on the part of, by

entries.meaning: Puts the subject in the position of the one to whom something is done. It is a sympathy device: the grammar makes the subject an active noun while the meaning makes it a patient.
examples: Small suppliers are usually on the receiving end of these renegotiations.
He has been on the receiving end of two lawsuits from the same tenant.
Nobody wants to be on the receiving end of one of her performance reviews.
Referees are on the receiving end of abuse for ninety minutes a week.
She found herself on the receiving end of a very public apology.
The town was on the receiving end of every storm that came up the valley.
entries.русский: на принимающей стороне, тот, на ком это отыгралось — с оттенком сочувствия
entries.register: informal to neutral; conversation and journalism
entries.complement: noun phrase, almost always naming something unpleasant — a lawsuit, a tirade, a beating, a joke. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: be/find oneself on the receiving end of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The phrase is negatively loaded by default: on the receiving end of a raise sounds wrong, while on the receiving end of a lecture sounds exactly right, and a positive object is heard as irony. Against plain receive, it moves the subject into the patient's position and quietly asks for sympathy. Against at the hands of, which is graver and names the agent, this one names the act. The mirror phrase on the giving end exists but is far rarer and usually appears only to complete the contrast.
entries.see also: at the hands of, at the mercy of, in the face of, on the part of, subject to

entries.meaning: Names the evidence or achievement that carried a decision. It presupposes that somebody was persuaded, which is why it attaches to hirings, loans, verdicts, promotions, and signings.
examples: The loan was approved on the strength of two years of receipts.
She was promoted on the strength of a single quarter.
On the strength of his testimony, the charges were refiled.
The band was signed on the strength of a four-song demo.
The town rebuilt its budget on the strength of what the new plant paid in taxes.
He got the fellowship on the strength of one unpublished chapter.
entries.pronunciation note: connected speech /ɑn ðə ˈstrɛŋk θə/ · on thuh STRENGKTH uhv
entries.русский: на основании, опираясь на — довод или заслуга, решившие дело
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative (on the strength of what the scouts reported). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the strength of [noun phrase]. · On the strength of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Against on the basis of, which names a criterion neutrally, on the strength of adds that the thing named was persuasive enough to carry the decision: hired on the basis of her portfolio says the portfolio was what they looked at, hired on the strength of her portfolio says it was what convinced them. Against because of, it confines the cause to evidence, testimony, or a record that somebody actually weighed. It resists a weak object — on the strength of a rumor reads as deliberate irony, and that irony is the proof of the rule.
entries.see also: on the basis of, by virtue of, in light of, because of, on the strength of

entries.meaning: Places the subject one step short of a change of state. Because the change has not happened, the phrase stays true even if it never does.
examples: The company was on the verge of bankruptcy when the order came in.
She was on the verge of tears and would not look up.
Researchers say they are on the verge of a usable test.
He was on the verge of quitting when the transfer came through.
Two of the three species are on the verge of disappearing from the river.
The talks are on the verge of collapse for the third time this year.
entries.русский: на грани, вот-вот — в шаге от перемены состояния, которая может и не произойти
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (on the verge of collapse, on the verge of collapsing). Because of is a preposition, on the verge of to collapse is wrong, and so is on the verge to collapse. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: be on the verge of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · bring/push someone to the verge of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: on the brink of is the near-twin and is preferred for large disasters (on the brink of war); on the point of is the more formal, British-leaning version and takes the same gerund. The of is not optional — the elliptical She was on the verge survives only where the complement has just been said.
entries.contrast: Against sense 3 of close to (close to tears), which is gradable and vague about the outcome, on the verge of names a threshold about to be crossed, and it takes only outcomes, never places: close to the airport is fine, on the verge of the airport is nonsense. Against in danger of, it is neutral about whether the outcome is welcome — you can be on the verge of a breakthrough as easily as a breakdown, where in danger of is always bad.
entries.see also: close to, in danger of, short of, in the process of, up against

examples: The keys are on top of the refrigerator.
The truck stopped right on top of the crosswalk.
Stack the folders on top of the printer for now.
On top of everything else, the furnace quit.
On top of paying rent, they cover their own utilities.
She stays on top of every deadline without visible effort.
The manager is completely on top of the situation.

senses.head: Resting on the upper surface of
body: The keys are on top of the refrigerator.

senses.head: In addition to (usually burdensome)
body: On top of everything else, the car wouldn't start.

senses.head: In full control of; up to date with
body: She stays on top of every deadline.
examples: The keys are on top of the refrigerator.
The truck stopped right on top of the crosswalk.
Stack the folders on top of the printer for now.
On top of everything else, the furnace quit.
On top of paying rent, they cover their own utilities.
She stays on top of every deadline without visible effort.
The manager is completely on top of the situation.

entries.русский: на, поверх; тж. вдобавок к (обычно обременительно); тж. держащий под полным контролем
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund in sense 2 (on top of paying rent). Sense 3 also takes a nominal wh-clause (on top of what the auditors want). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] on top of [noun phrase] · On top of [noun phrase], [clause]. · right on top of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Sense 1 is literal and takes intensifiers (right on top of); senses 2 and 3 are frozen idioms. Against in addition to, sense 2 is the informal equivalent and usually carries a complaint — things pile on top of each other. Against above, sense 1 requires contact: a lamp above the table is not touching it; a book on top of the table is. Bare on top is an adverb, not this preposition, and takes no object: The cake had berries on top is complete; on top of the cake needs its object.
entries.see also: in addition to, as well as, in front of, in charge of, on

Get the dog out of the kitchen.
The whole sculpture is carved out of a single log.

entries.русский: из (изнутри, из источника, из материала); из числа; без (кончилось); из (побуждения); вне
entries.register: neutral — one of the most frequent prepositions in the language
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; a gerund in sense 5 only (out of not wanting to offend anyone). In senses 4 and 5 the complement is characteristically a bare mass or abstract noun (out of milk, out of curiosity). Never a that-clause; a nominal wh-clause is possible in sense 2 (out of what little was left).
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] out of [noun phrase] · be out of [noun phrase] · [number] out of [number] · made out of [material]
entries.contrast: Out alone is an adverb or a verb particle and takes no object (She went out, Cross it out); out of is the preposition and requires one. Against from, sense 1 insists on prior enclosure — you come out of a building but from a city. Against of, sense 3 (made out of wood) stresses transformation of raw material, where made of wood just names the substance.
entries.see also: outside of, inside of, away from, short of, of, from

examples: The plant is just outside of the city limits.
That question falls outside of the committee's mandate.
She has no life outside of work.
Outside of a sore shoulder, I feel fine.
Outside of Chicago, he's never lived in a big city.
There's nothing to do here outside of fish and read.

senses.head: Beyond the limits of (spatial or figurative; the of is dispensable)
body: The plant is outside of the city limits.

senses.head: Except for; apart from (American, informal)
body: Outside of a sore shoulder, I feel fine.
examples: The plant is just outside of the city limits.
That question falls outside of the committee's mandate.
She has no life outside of work.
Outside of a sore shoulder, I feel fine.

entries.русский: за пределами, вне (of необязательно); тж. амер. разг. кроме, если не считать
entries.register: neutral in sense 1 (with the of often edited out); informal and chiefly American in sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (sense 2: outside of going to the store), or a nominal wh-clause (outside of what has already been said). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] outside of [noun phrase] · Outside of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: In the spatial sense the of is optional and edited American prose usually drops it — outside the building, not outside of the building. Sense 2, meaning "except for," is an Americanism that many editors also cut in favor of aside from or except for, but it is fully idiomatic in speech. Bare outside is an adverb: Wait outside.
entries.see also: inside of, out of, aside from, apart from, except for

entries.meaning: Declares a factor immaterial to what the main clause asserts. Because it takes wh-clauses freely, it is unusually flexible for a complex preposition.
examples: The policy applies to all students regardless of age.
Regardless of the weather, the parade steps off at noon.
She'll say the same thing regardless of who is in the room.
The fee is due regardless of whether you attend.
Regardless of cost, this has to be fixed before winter.
He was going to resign regardless of the vote.
entries.русский: независимо от, невзирая на — фактор объявляется неважным; форма irregardless нелитературна
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (regardless of what happens, regardless of whether he agrees). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] regardless of [noun phrase / wh-clause]. · Regardless of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Irregardless is not a word in standard English — it is a blend of irrespective and regardless, and although dictionaries record it, it is stigmatized everywhere and should never be written. Against in spite of and despite, regardless of dismisses a factor as irrelevant rather than conceding it as an obstacle: in spite of the cost admits the cost was a problem, regardless of the cost refuses to weigh it. Bare regardless is an adverb: He went anyway, regardless.
entries.see also: irrespective of, in spite of, notwithstanding, in the face of

entries.русский: без, при нехватке (до нужного); не доходя до (отметки); кроме как, разве что (чудо)
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (short of firing him), or a nominal wh-clause (short of what organizers predicted). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: be short of [noun phrase] · [clause] short of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · just/well/little short of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Three senses that share a metaphor of falling before a line. Sense 3, "apart from doing," is the one learners miss: Short of selling the house, we've tried everything means "we have tried everything except that." Against out of, sense 1 means "not enough," where out of means "none at all" — short of milk versus out of milk. Bare short is an adjective or adverb and takes no object: We came up short, He stopped short, The fund is short again — where short of always requires one.
entries.see also: out of, in need of, devoid of, save for, but for

entries.meaning: Limits an assertion to what the speaker knows or can do. Its natural home is the affidavit, where it converts an absolute claim into a survivable one.
examples: To the best of my knowledge, no such payment was ever authorized.
She performed the work to the best of her ability under impossible deadlines.
To the best of our recollection, the meeting lasted about twenty minutes.
The verification reads: true to the best of my knowledge, information, and belief.
To the best of anyone's judgment, the building was empty at the time.
He answered every question to the best of his understanding of what was being asked.
entries.pronunciation note: to reduces to /tə/ and the st+of cluster simplifies · tuh thuh BEST uhv
entries.русский: насколько (мне известно, я могу) — ограничивает утверждение знанием говорящего
entries.register: formal to neutral; affidavits, sworn testimony, and careful correspondence
entries.complement: a possessive noun phrase and nothing else — to the best of my knowledge, to the best of her ability, to the best of our recollection. Never a that-clause, never a gerund, and never a bare noun: to the best of knowledge is not English. The noun after the possessive comes from a very short list: knowledge, ability, belief, recollection, information, judgment, understanding.
entries.pattern: To the best of [possessive] knowledge, [clause]. · [clause] to the best of [possessive] ability.
entries.contrast: This is a hedge, and in a sworn statement it is a legally meaningful one: to the best of my knowledge is what lets an affiant swear to something without swearing that it is objectively true. Against as far as I know, it is the formal equivalent; against I think, it claims diligence rather than mere opinion. The tripled formula to the best of my knowledge, information, and belief is standard verification language on pleadings. Note that this to is prepositional, so the unit is a prepositional phrase and can never be followed by a verb.
entries.see also: to the satisfaction of, according to, as far as, to the extent of, in witness whereof

entries.meaning: Names the party entitled to be paid, and by naming them in this particular way makes the instrument transferable. It is probably the most-printed complex preposition in American life and among the least examined.
examples: The check is made payable to the order of the Marion County Treasurer.
Pay to the order of bearer, and whoever holds it can cash it.
The note was endorsed to the order of the assignee bank.
Draw the draft to the order of the escrow agent, not the seller.
Instruments payable to the order of a named person are negotiable; those payable simply to that person are not.
Compare on the order of, which means "roughly" and has nothing to do with payment.
entries.русский: приказу (такого-то) — фин./юр.; на чеке и векселе, делает документ передаваемым
entries.register: formal; banking and negotiable instruments. An American reads it every time a check is written.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the payee. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: Pay to the order of [noun phrase] (the formula printed on every American check) · made payable to the order of [noun phrase] · endorsed to the order of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with on the order of, which means "approximately": on the order of ten thousand dollars is an estimate, while to the order of names a payee. The words to the order of are what make an instrument negotiable — a check payable to John Doe is payable to him, while one payable to the order of John Doe can be endorsed over to somebody else. Against plain to, then, the difference is legal and real, which is why the phrase is preprinted rather than left to the writer.
entries.see also: in favor of, for the account of, in trust for, care of, on the order of

entries.meaning: States how far a quality or a process went by naming the extreme it arrived at. It is nearly always evaluative: the point named is meant to sound like too much.
examples: He is thorough to the point of obsession.
The instructions were simplified to the point of being useless.
She pushed the argument to the point of absurdity and then kept going.
The mine flooded to the point of collapse before anyone was pulled out.
Rehearsals ran to the point of exhaustion for the entire cast.
Rents rose to the point of driving the last grocery store out of the neighborhood.
entries.русский: до (такой степени, что) — называет крайность, до которой дошло; обычно с осуждением
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (to the point of losing customers), and the gerund is very common. Never a that-clause and never a bare infinitive — to the point of lose customers is wrong, because this to is a preposition, not an infinitive marker.
entries.pattern: [gradable adjective or verb] to the point of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · almost to the point of [noun phrase] · to the point of absurdity / exhaustion / tears (fixed collocations)
entries.contrast: It marks a degree reached, so it needs something gradable in front of it: thorough to the point of obsession, polite to the point of coldness. Against so ... that, which takes a clause, this takes a noun or an -ing form — so tired that he fell asleep versus tired to the point of falling asleep. Against on the verge of, which says the outcome has not happened, to the point of says the degree was actually arrived at. The clause-taking counterpart is the conjunction to the point that (or to the point where), and that is the workaround when a clause is what you need.
entries.see also: on the verge of, in excess of, short of, up to, to the extent of

entries.meaning: Names whoever must approve before an obligation counts as performed. It is a small allocation of power, and negotiators treat it as one.
examples: The work must be completed to the satisfaction of the city engineer.
Repairs were made to the satisfaction of the inspector and the insurer both.
The evidence must establish the fact to the satisfaction of the trier of fact.
The site shall be restored to the reasonable satisfaction of the landowner.
Nothing was ever finished to the satisfaction of that particular client.
To the satisfaction of names who decides; in satisfaction of names what is discharged.
entries.русский: к удовлетворению (кого-то) — чьё одобрение требуется, чтобы обязательство считалось исполненным
entries.register: formal; construction contracts, regulatory approvals, and closing conditions
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the person or body who has to be satisfied. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: performed/completed to the satisfaction of [noun phrase] · to the reasonable satisfaction of [noun phrase] (the negotiated form)
entries.contrast: The complement is the judge of the work, not the standard applied — to the satisfaction of the city engineer means the engineer decides. Against in satisfaction of, which discharges a debt, this one sets an approval condition; the two share a noun and nothing else. In drafting, the word to watch for is reasonable: bare to the satisfaction of the buyer hands the buyer an unreviewable veto, and to the reasonable satisfaction of the buyer is what the seller's lawyer will insist on putting back in.
entries.see also: in satisfaction of, to the best of, subject to, under the terms of, in accordance with

entries.meaning: Attaches a named punishment to a statement or an act. In the perjury formula the phrase is performative: signing under it is what makes a false statement a crime.
examples: I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing is true and correct.
The tag reads: not to be removed under penalty of law.
Witnesses were ordered to appear under penalty of contempt.
Firearms may not be carried past this point under penalty of forfeiture.
Sign the declaration under penalty of perjury or have it notarized; either satisfies the rule.
The older literary form is on pain of, as in on pain of death.
entries.русский: под страхом (наказания) — юр.; привязывает названную кару к заявлению или действию
entries.register: formal; statutes, sworn declarations, and government forms
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the sanction — perjury, law, forfeiture, contempt, death. Never a that-clause and never a gerund. In the fixed formulas the complement is article-less: under penalty of perjury, under penalty of law.
entries.pattern: declare/sign under penalty of perjury (fixed) · [prohibition] under penalty of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: on pain of and under pain of are the older and more literary equivalents (on pain of death); under penalty of is the American statutory form.
entries.contrast: Two distinct uses. In I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing is true, it attaches a consequence to a statement — and that sentence, from 28 U.S.C. § 1746, is why an unsworn federal declaration can stand in for a notarized affidavit. In Do not remove under penalty of law, it attaches a consequence to a prohibition, and the mattress tag is the version nearly every American has actually read. Against subject to, which names an exposure in general terms, this one names the specific punishment.
entries.see also: under the authority of, subject to, in violation of, pursuant to, under

entries.meaning: Names the institution whose protection or sponsorship covers the activity. Choose it over under the auspices of only when you want the note of shelter rather than of endorsement.
examples: The dig proceeded under the aegis of the national museum.
Three journals are published under the aegis of the same learned society.
The talks were held under the aegis of a neutral third country.
Her research went on for a decade under the aegis of a foundation that no longer exists.
The festival now operates under the aegis of the city's arts commission.
It is EE-jiss, not EYE-jiss, and the plural aegises is best avoided.
entries.pronunciation note: UN-dur thee EE-jiss uhv — the ae is /i/, and EYE-jiss is a mispronunciation
entries.русский: под эгидой, под защитой — книжн.; акцент на покровительстве и укрытии
entries.register: formal and slightly literary; scholarship, institutional writing, and arts journalism
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a protecting or sponsoring institution or person. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] under the aegis of [noun phrase] · operate/publish/work under the aegis of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: under the auspices of means the same thing and is far commoner; under the umbrella of is the informal equivalent.
entries.contrast: Aegis is the shield of Zeus, lent to Athena, and the metaphor is protection — which is the shade of difference from under the auspices of, where the metaphor is Roman bird-augury and the emphasis falls on sponsorship and approval. In practice American writers treat them as interchangeable and reach for auspices far more often. The pronunciation is where people come to grief: /ˈidʒɪs/, not /ˈaɪdʒɪs/. It is a classical borrowing and it sounds like one, so it suits scholarly and institutional prose and sounds inflated anywhere else.
entries.see also: under the auspices of, under the authority of, by leave of, courtesy of, under

entries.meaning: Names the body sponsoring or authorizing the activity. American readers meet it most often in datelines about international negotiations and in grant and program language.
examples: The talks were convened under the auspices of the United Nations.
The survey was carried out under the auspices of the state historical society.
Six clinics operate under the auspices of the county health department.
The exchange program runs under the auspices of a bilateral cultural agreement.
Under the auspices of a small grant, she spent two years in the archives.
The noun is always plural: auspices, never auspice.
entries.русский: под эгидой, при содействии — организация-устроитель или санкционирующая сторона
entries.register: formal; institutional, diplomatic, and academic writing
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the sponsoring body. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] under the auspices of [noun phrase] · held/convened/funded under the auspices of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The plainest English equivalents are sponsored by and organized by, and in ordinary prose those are better; under the auspices of earns its length where the sponsor's authority is itself part of the news, since talks under the auspices of the United Nations are different talks from talks held in a hotel. Against under the aegis of, it is commoner and stresses sponsorship rather than protection. The noun is plural and stays plural: under the auspice of is an error. The auspices were originally the omens read from the flight of birds before a Roman undertaking, which is why the phrase still carries a faint sense of official blessing.
entries.see also: under the aegis of, under the authority of, courtesy of, by virtue of, under color of

entries.meaning: Names the source of the power being exercised. It answers the question "who says you may?" — which in American administrative law is very often the whole case.
examples: The rule was issued under the authority of Section 5 of the Act.
The task force operates under the authority of the attorney general.
Inspectors entered under the authority of a warrant signed that morning.
The clinic dispenses under the authority of a supervising physician.
Under the authority of the emergency declaration, the county closed the roads.
Compare under color of authority, which claims the power was only apparent.
entries.русский: на основании полномочий, по уполномочию — источник осуществляемой власти
entries.register: formal; statutes, agency notices, and institutional writing
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person, an office, or a legal instrument. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [act] under the authority of [noun phrase] · acting under the authority of [noun phrase] · issued under the authority of [statute]
entries.contrast: Two kinds of complement, two meanings. With a person or office, it means subordinate to them (the task force operates under the authority of the attorney general). With a statute or instrument, it means "as that law empowers," and there pursuant to and by virtue of are the closer synonyms. Against under the auspices of, which is about sponsorship, this one is about power: auspices bless, authority commands. Against under color of, which alleges that the authority was only apparent, this one asserts that it was real.
entries.see also: pursuant to, by virtue of, under the auspices of, under the aegis of, under color of, under and pursuant to

entries.meaning: Attributes a rule or an obligation to a particular instrument. Its natural sentence explains a deal: it opens the paragraph and tells the reader that what follows is what the document says.
examples: Under the terms of the settlement, the company admits no wrongdoing.
Employees keep their seniority under the terms of the new contract.
Under the terms of her will, the farm passes to the county land trust.
The country agreed to inspections under the terms of the 2015 accord.
Under the terms of the license, the software may not be redistributed.
The plural matters: under the terms of the lease, never under the term of the lease.
entries.русский: по условиям (договора) — приписывает обязанность конкретному документу
entries.register: formal to neutral; contracts, settlements, and the business and political press
entries.complement: noun phrase naming an instrument — an agreement, a settlement, a treaty, a will, a license. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: Under the terms of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] under the terms of [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The noun is plural: under the terms of the settlement, not under the term of, which would mean "during the term" and is a different statement entirely. Against bare under, which does the same work in one word (under the settlement, the company pays $4 million), the longer form is the reporter's version and is often cuttable. Against pursuant to, it is the plain-English choice and the better one outside drafting; against in accordance with, it points at a specific document rather than at a standard.
entries.see also: pursuant to, in accordance with, subject to, under the authority of, by virtue of

entries.meaning: Declares emptiness of a quality. Where devoid of still functions in edited prose, void of signals deliberate archaism.
examples: His face was void of expression.
The landscape was void of color for four straight months.
The reply was polite and entirely void of content.
He looked at her with eyes void of recognition.
The document is void of any signature or seal.
entries.русский: лишённый — нарочито устар.; живой современный вариант — devoid of
entries.register: archaic and literary; survives in legal boilerplate
entries.complement: noun phrase only, almost always abstract. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: be void of [noun phrase] · [noun] void of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Devoid of is the living modern form and should be preferred in every ordinary context; void of now reads as poetic or as legal survival. Do not confuse with the legal adjective void meaning "of no effect" (the contract is void), which takes no of.
entries.see also: devoid of, in the absence of, short of, exclusive of

entries.meaning: Says the subject has been worn into acceptance of something by exposure to it. It is freely gradable — more accustomed, not yet accustomed, thoroughly accustomed — which is what still marks accustomed as a live adjective rather than a fully frozen particle.
examples: She is accustomed to working nights and sleeps through the afternoon.
He never grew accustomed to the cold.
Readers accustomed to the old layout complained for months.
They are not accustomed to being questioned.
It took a full year to become accustomed to the altitude.
A jury accustomed to long trials would not have found this one unusual.
He is quite accustomed to having his calls returned within the hour.
entries.русский: привыкший к — далее существительное или -ing, никогда не инфинитив
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund only. The to is a preposition, not an infinitive marker, so accustomed to work nights is wrong — it must be accustomed to working nights. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause. The reflexive verb form accustom oneself to follows exactly the same rule: accustom yourself to waiting, never to wait.
entries.pattern: be/grow/become accustomed to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · [noun] accustomed to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · quite/hardly/not yet accustomed to [noun phrase]
entries.beware the trap: used to + bare infinitive (He used to live alone) is a completely different item, a past-habitual auxiliary, and the collision of the two is the reason learners produce I'm used to live here.
entries.variants: used to is the everyday equivalent and takes the identical complement — used to living alone, never used to live alone in this sense.
entries.contrast: This is the cleanest test case in the file for the prepositional to. Substitute a plain noun: accustomed to the noise is perfectly good, which proves the to is a preposition and forces the -ing on any verb that follows. The same test convicts look forward to hearing and object to being questioned. Against given to (given to exaggeration), which reports a tendency, accustomed to reports habituation through repeated exposure. Against familiar with, which is about knowledge, this is about tolerance.
entries.see also: subject to, opposed to, obedient to, close to, up to

entries.meaning: Reports that somebody is willing to go along with what follows. It is the correspondence word, and it belongs to the small group of adjectives whose to is prepositional and therefore demands an -ing form.
examples: Both parties are agreeable to a thirty-day extension.
Let me know whether Thursday at ten is agreeable to you.
The seller was agreeable to closing before the end of the month.
She is agreeable to almost anything except moving the deadline again.
The terms proved agreeable to everyone but the insurer.
The old sense survives in documents: the plat was made agreeable to the act of 1789.

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund in sense 3 (close to quitting), or a nominal wh-clause (close to what we expected). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive: close to finishing, not close to finish.

entries.meaning: States that one thing matches or accords with another. Learn it for reading older documents; write consistent with.
examples: The conduct complained of was conformable to the custom of the trade.
He held the practice conformable to both statute and precedent.
The survey lines are conformable to those returned in 1802.
Locke asks whether our ideas are conformable to the things themselves.
The upper beds are conformable to the shale below, with no break in deposition.
A modern writer would say consistent with in every one of these but the last.
entries.русский: сообразный с, соответствующий — устар.; сегодня пишут consistent with
entries.register: formal and archaic; eighteenth- and nineteenth-century legal, scientific, and philosophical prose, surviving today in geology and in quotation
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Because the to is prepositional, conformable to follow the rule is wrong; the grammatical form is conformable to following the rule, though the sentence is better rewritten. Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [thing] is conformable to [noun phrase] · [noun] conformable to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: conformable with occurs and is rarer; the ordinary modern equivalents are consistent with, in accordance with, and plain matching.
entries.contrast: A period word. Where an eighteenth-century writer said conformable to the laws of nature, a modern one says consistent with, and using conformable to in current prose reads as antiquarian rather than precise. One live technical use remains: in geology, strata are conformable when they were laid down without interruption, and there the word is ordinary shop talk. Distinguish the verb conform, which is entirely alive and takes to (conform to the specification), from this adjective, which is not.
entries.see also: agreeable to, in accordance with, in keeping with, pursuant to, consistent with

entries.the classic test: due to is traditionally adjectival, so it should be substitutable by attributable to or caused by and should attach to a noun — The delay was due to fog (fine, due to modifies delay). Using it adverbially to modify a whole clause — Due to fog, the flight was canceled — was condemned for most of the twentieth century, and because of or owing to was prescribed instead. That adverbial use is now standard in American English and appears in edited prose everywhere, but conservative editors still flag it, so because of is the safe choice in formal writing.
