entries.pattern: [clause] next to [noun phrase] · Next to [noun phrase], [clause]. · next to [negative quantifier]
entries.contrast: Against beside, which means the same thing and is one word shorter, next to is the more common in American speech. ✗ Do not confuse beside with besides: beside is the spatial word, "at the side of," while besides means "in addition to" or "apart from" (Besides the rent, there's insurance). The fixed idiom is beside the point, meaning irrelevant — and besides the point is simply an error for it, not a phrase with a meaning of its own. Against close to, next to requires immediate adjacency — nothing between the two things. Sense 2, next to nothing, is a fixed idiom meaning "almost none" and has no spatial content; sense 3 is comparative and means "compared with." ✗ Bare next is a determiner or an adverb and takes no object — next week, Who's next?, the house next door — where the preposition always has one.
entries.see also: close to, next door to, in front of, ahead of, alongside, on top of

entries.meaning: Says the subject submits to an authority, a law, or a principle. It is the vocabulary of scripture, oaths, and nineteenth-century prose, and outside those settings it sounds antique.
examples: The design is obedient to the constraints of the site.
A citizen is obedient to the law, not to the officer enforcing it.
The prose is obedient to a rhythm that never varies.
He remained obedient to the vows he had taken at twenty.
Every part of the machine is obedient to a single cam.
entries.русский: покорный, послушный — книжн./устар.; о подчинении власти, закону, принципу
entries.type: complex (adjective + fixed preposition; marginal — it is closer to an adjective governing its complement than to a true unit)
entries.complement: noun phrase only. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund — and, the to being a preposition, never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: be obedient to [noun phrase] · [noun] obedient to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Listed here because it patterns like contrary to and pursuant to, but it is the weakest member of the family: obedient is a fully live adjective and to is simply the preposition it takes, so the two do not fuse the way according to does. Compare subject to, which has fused much further and has developed meanings the adjective subject no longer carries on its own. In modern American prose, obeys or complies with is nearly always better.
entries.see also: subject to, accustomed to, pursuant to, contrary to, in accordance with, according to

entries.meaning: States that the subject holds a position of resistance. Because it is a participial adjective rather than a verb, it reports a settled stance rather than an act of opposing, which is why committees and editorial pages reach for it.
examples: Two members are firmly opposed to the merger.
She is opposed to raising the fee in an election year.
The union is not opposed to automation as such.
He remained bitterly opposed to the settlement until the last day.
Voters opposed to the measure outnumbered its supporters two to one.
They are opposed to being surveyed at all.
Nobody on the board is opposed to the idea in principle.
entries.русский: выступающий против — устоявшаяся позиция, а не сам акт противодействия
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund only. The to is a preposition, so opposed to raise the fee is wrong — it must be opposed to raising the fee. Never a that-clause; a nominal wh-clause is marginal and best avoided.
entries.pattern: be/remain opposed to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · [noun] opposed to [noun phrase] · strongly/bitterly/firmly/implacably opposed to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Distinguish this sharply from as opposed to, which is a different item doing a different job: She is opposed to the plan states a position, while a grant, as opposed to a loan draws a definitional line and states no position at all. Dropping the as changes the sentence from a clarification into an assertion of belief, and the two are confused constantly. Against plain against, which is shorter and says the same thing (She is against the plan), opposed to is the formal register's choice and grades more freely. Against in favor of, it is the exact antonym and takes the same complements.
entries.see also: as opposed to, in favor of, contrary to, subject to, accustomed to

entries.meaning: Places one thing facing or inverting another. American writers should prefer across from for places and the opposite of for abstractions.
examples: The effect was exactly opposite to what the designers intended.
Their conclusions are opposite to ours in every particular.
The pharmacy sits opposite to the courthouse. (chiefly British; American: across from)
Warm air moves opposite to the surface current.
Her instinct runs opposite to his on almost every question.
entries.русский: напротив, противоположный — в амер. письме лучше across from или the opposite of
entries.register: formal; chiefly British in the spatial sense
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a nominal wh-clause in the abstract sense (opposite to what the designers intended). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [noun/clause] opposite to [noun phrase / wh-clause]
entries.variants: In American English the ordinary spatial word is bare opposite (the house opposite ours) or, far more often, across from (the house across from ours). Opposite to survives in American usage mainly in the abstract sense "the reverse of."
entries.contrast: Bare opposite is itself a preposition and needs no to; adding to is a British habit in the spatial sense and is redundant in American prose. Against in front of, opposite requires the two things to face each other across a space. Against contrary to, which asserts conflict, opposite to asserts inversion.
entries.see also: in front of, contrary to, as opposed to, next to

entries.meaning: Names the cause of the situation in the main clause. Its safety in the sentence-adverbial position is its whole reason for surviving alongside because of.
examples: Owing to a scheduling conflict, the hearing was moved to Thursday.
The shortfall is owing to lower-than-expected enrollment.
Owing to the drought, the district imposed watering restrictions.
Several flights were delayed owing to a systems failure at the tower.
Owing to being closed for renovation, the branch is not accepting returns.
entries.русский: из-за, вследствие — как because of, но свободно стоит в начале предложения
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (owing to what the survey found). Never a that-clause — owing to the fact that is the clause-taking workaround. The to is a preposition, so never a bare infinitive: owing to being closed, not owing to be closed.
entries.pattern: Owing to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] owing to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Owing to is the preposition that traditionalists prescribe instead of adverbial due to: Owing to fog, the flight was canceled has never been disputed, while Due to fog, ... has. The two are otherwise synonymous, and both mean because of. In American English owing to is noticeably more formal and less frequent than in British English.
entries.see also: due to, because of, on account of, as a result of, thanks to

entries.meaning: Places an event earlier than another. Its one real advantage over before is that it cannot be misread as spatial.
examples: All applications must be received prior to the March 1 deadline.
Prior to signing, read the arbitration clause carefully.
She had no experience in the field prior to 2019.
Employees hired prior to the merger keep their original benefits.
Prior to the storm, the reservoir was already at capacity.
entries.русский: до, перед — офиц.; в отличие от before не читается как «впереди» в пространстве
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (prior to signing). Never a bare infinitive — prior to sign the lease is wrong — and never a that-clause or a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] prior to [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · Prior to [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Prior to means before, and before is almost always better. It is the most reliably flagged padding in this whole family; usage guides from Fowler onward have called it a needless formality. Keep it only where before would be ambiguous with the spatial sense, or in legal drafting where it is conventional. Note that prior alone is an adjective (a prior conviction), not a preposition.
entries.see also: subsequent to, ahead of, as of, in advance of, pending, before

entries.meaning: Grounds an action in the legal authority that permits it. It is one of the few prepositions in English whose register is essentially a single profession.
examples: The subpoena was issued pursuant to Rule 45.
Pursuant to the settlement agreement, the payments begin in January.
Records are released pursuant to a valid public-records request.
The officer conducted the search pursuant to a warrant.
Pursuant to state law, the notice must run for three consecutive weeks.
entries.русский: во исполнение, согласно, на основании — юр.; ссылка на правовое основание действия
entries.register: legal — essentially confined to statutes, contracts, and court filings
entries.complement: noun phrase only, almost always a legal instrument. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund, and never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: [clause] pursuant to [noun phrase]. · Pursuant to [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Means "under, in accordance with, as authorized by." Against in accordance with, it is narrower — the object must be a rule or authority that empowers the action, not merely a standard the action matched. Plain-language drafting guides recommend under in nearly every case: under Section 12 says what pursuant to Section 12 says.
entries.see also: in accordance with, by virtue of, subject to, under, on the basis of, in receipt of

examples: Wages have fallen sharply relative to housing costs.
The fund underperformed relative to its benchmark for the third year running.
Motion is only meaningful relative to a chosen frame of reference.
The city's crime rate is low relative to comparable metros.
The memo raises several questions relative to the proposed timeline.
Please forward any documents relative to the 2023 audit.

senses.head: In comparison with; measured against
body: Wages have fallen relative to housing costs.

senses.head: Concerning; with regard to
body: The memo raises questions relative to the timeline.
examples: Wages have fallen sharply relative to housing costs.
The fund underperformed relative to its benchmark for the third year running.
Motion is only meaningful relative to a chosen frame of reference.
The city's crime rate is low relative to comparable metros.
The memo raises several questions relative to the proposed timeline.
Please forward any documents relative to the 2023 audit.

entries.русский: по отношению к, по сравнению с; тж. касательно, относительно (темы)
entries.register: formal; technical in sense 1, bureaucratic in sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (relative to what we paid last year). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: [clause] relative to [noun phrase] · Relative to [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Sense 1 is quantitative and is the standard scientific and financial word for a benchmark comparison. Sense 2 means "concerning" and is stiff bureaucratic English for about — the same criticism that applies to in terms of and with regard to. Against compared with, sense 1 implies a proportional or normalized comparison, not just a side-by-side one.
entries.see also: in comparison with, in relation to, with respect to, as opposed to, in terms of

entries.meaning: Asserts resemblance without asserting identity. Because it is gradable, the real information is usually in the adverb in front of it rather than in the phrase itself.
examples: The new policy is similar to one Ohio adopted in 2019.
Her handwriting is strikingly similar to her mother's.
Running a clinic is similar to running a small business, only with worse hours.
The symptoms are broadly similar to what we saw last winter.
This one is similar to mine but a generation older.
The two proposals are similar to each other in everything but price.
entries.pronunciation note: SIM-uh-lur too — not /ˈsɪmjələr/; there is no y sound in it
entries.русский: похожий на, подобный — сходство без тождества; смысл обычно в наречии перед ним
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (similar to mine), gerund (similar to running a small business), or a free relative (similar to what we saw last year). Never a that-clause, and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive: similar to filing, not similar to file.
entries.pattern: [X] is similar to [Y] · very / broadly / roughly / strikingly similar to [noun phrase] · [noun] similar to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Similar to takes to; different from takes from — two exact opposites with opposite prepositions, and both similar with and similar than are errors. Against like, the one-word preposition doing the same job (a car like mine), similar to is the written, hedged form and grades freely in a way like cannot: broadly similar to has no like equivalent. Against the same as, it deliberately stops short of identity — things similar to each other are not claimed to match.
entries.see also: different from, close to, relative to, in comparison with, similar to, like

examples: Late filings are subject to a fifty-dollar penalty.
All imports are subject to inspection at the port of entry.
Contractors are subject to the same conduct code as employees.
The valley is subject to flash flooding every spring.
He has been subject to migraines since his twenties.
Prices are subject to change without notice.
The sale is subject to financing and a clean inspection.
The appointment is subject to being confirmed by the full council.

senses.head: Liable to; exposed to (a charge, penalty, or requirement)
body: Late filings are subject to a fifty-dollar penalty.

senses.head: Prone to; repeatedly affected by
body: The valley is subject to flash flooding.

senses.head: Conditional on; not final until (contract language)
body: The sale is subject to financing.
examples: Late filings are subject to a fifty-dollar penalty.
All imports are subject to inspection at the port of entry.
Contractors are subject to the same conduct code as employees.
The valley is subject to flash flooding every spring.
He has been subject to migraines since his twenties.
Prices are subject to change without notice.
The sale is subject to financing and a clean inspection.
The appointment is subject to being confirmed by the full council.

entries.pronunciation note: SUB-jikt too — adjective stress on the first syllable; the verb subject is /səbˈdʒɛkt/, sub-JEKT
entries.русский: подлежащий (штрафу), подверженный (наводнениям); тж. при условии (одобрения)
entries.register: neutral to formal; sense 3 is the language of contracts and offers
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. The to is a preposition, so subject to be approved is wrong — write subject to being approved, or better, the nominal subject to approval. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: be subject to [noun phrase] · [noun phrase], subject to [noun phrase] · subject to change / approval / availability / audit (fixed collocations)
entries.contrast: Three senses a reader must keep apart, because only the third makes the surrounding statement provisional: The offer is final, subject to board approval is not a final offer, and the whole force of the sentence sits in those three words. Sense 1 is liability, sense 2 is disposition, sense 3 is conditionality. Watch the stress and the part of speech — subjected to is the passive verb and means "made to undergo" (subjected to questioning), which is not this item. Against obedient to, which never fused, subject to has developed meanings the adjective subject no longer carries alone; against pursuant to, it names a condition rather than an authorizing rule.
entries.see also: obedient to, accustomed to, pursuant to, in accordance with, in violation of, depending on

entries.meaning: Places an event later than another. Like prior to, its persistence owes more to the gravity of official registers than to any distinction it draws.
examples: Subsequent to the merger, three regional offices were closed.
No changes were made subsequent to the final review.
Claims filed subsequent to the deadline will not be considered.
Subsequent to filing the report, the auditor discovered a second error.
The property was rezoned subsequent to the 2019 general plan update.
entries.русский: после, вслед за — канц.; то же, что after, только длиннее
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a bare infinitive — subsequent to filing, not subsequent to file.
entries.pattern: [clause] subsequent to [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · Subsequent to [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: The mirror image of prior to, and subject to the same criticism: after is shorter and clearer in nearly every sentence. It is genuinely useful only in accounting and legal contexts where subsequent events is a term of art. Note that subsequent alone is an adjective and takes no complement.
entries.see also: prior to, in the wake of, as of, following

entries.meaning: Attributes an outcome to a person or factor, with an evaluative charge that plain because of lacks. Read the surrounding sentence to know whether the charge is gratitude or sarcasm.
examples: Thanks to a last-minute donation, the shelter stayed open.
She finished the degree in three years thanks to summer courses.
The team is in the playoffs thanks to a kicker nobody had heard of in August.
Thanks to being warned a day early, we moved the equipment in time.
Thanks to you, we missed the exit and drove twenty miles the wrong way.
Thanks to one clause nobody read, the lease renews automatically.
We got there on time, no thanks to the detour signs.
The roof held, no thanks to the contractor who installed it.

senses.head: Because of (a welcome cause); with credit to
body: Thanks to a last-minute donation, the shelter stayed open.

senses.head: Because of (an unwelcome cause) — ironic, and equally common
body: Thanks to you, we missed the exit.

senses.head: no thanks to — despite the failure of (fixed)
body: We finished on time, no thanks to the detour signs.
examples: Thanks to a last-minute donation, the shelter stayed open.
She finished the degree in three years thanks to summer courses.
The team is in the playoffs thanks to a kicker nobody had heard of in August.
Thanks to being warned a day early, we moved the equipment in time.
Thanks to you, we missed the exit and drove twenty miles the wrong way.
Thanks to one clause nobody read, the lease renews automatically.
We got there on time, no thanks to the detour signs.
The roof held, no thanks to the contractor who installed it.

entries.русский: благодаря; тж. ирон. «спасибо» неприятной причине; no thanks to — отнюдь не благодаря
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund (thanks to being warned early), or a nominal wh-clause (thanks to what the neighbors did). Never a that-clause — the workaround is because.
entries.pattern: Thanks to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] thanks to [noun phrase]. · no thanks to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: A causal preposition that normally credits a welcome cause, which is what separates it from neutral because of. Its ironic use — Thanks to you, we missed the exit — is extremely common and depends entirely on tone; the fixed no thanks to (We finished on time, no thanks to him) makes the blame explicit. Do not confuse with the plural noun in give thanks to or with the greeting thanks to everyone who came, where thanks is a noun and to marks its recipient — the test is whether the sentence has a separate outcome being explained.
entries.see also: because of, due to, owing to, courtesy of, as a result of

examples: The theater holds up to four hundred people.
Fines run up to five thousand dollars per violation.
She walked up to the counter and asked for a refund.
The water came up to my knees before I turned back.
Everything went smoothly up to the last week of rehearsals.
Up to that point, she had never missed a shift.
What are those two up to in the garage?
He's been up to no good since he got here.
She wasn't up to a five-mile hike two months after surgery.
Nobody thought the rookie would be up to the pressure.
It's up to the board now, not to me.
Whether we go at all is up to the weather.

senses.head: As many or as much as; not exceeding (a ceiling)
body: The theater holds up to four hundred people.

senses.head: As far as; right up to (a point reached in space)
body: She walked up to the counter and asked for a refund.

senses.head: Until (a point in time)
body: Everything was fine up to the last week of rehearsals.

senses.head: Engaged in (usually something suspect)
body: What are those two up to?

senses.head: Capable of; equal to
body: He isn't up to the job.

senses.head: The responsibility or choice of
body: It's up to the board now.

entries.русский: до, не больше чем; вплоть до; чем занят (неладным); по силам; на чьё-то усмотрение
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund in sense 5 (up to running a marathon), or a nominal wh-clause in sense 6 (up to whoever signs off on it). Never a that-clause. In sense 4 the complement is nearly always a vague or negative noun (something, no good, what). Note that sense 6 also licenses a following to-infinitive on a separate subject — It's up to the board to decide — which is a different slot, not this preposition's complement.
entries.pattern: up to [quantity] · [verb of motion] up to [place] · be up to [noun phrase] · It's up to [person] to [verb] · be up to [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Up alone is an adverb or a particle (Stand up, Look it up); up to is the preposition and always has an object. Sense 1's "maximum" reading is a persistent source of advertising complaints: save up to 50% guarantees nothing, because it names a ceiling, not a floor. Sense 2 is the plain spatial one and is the sense the others are built out of — a limit reached and not passed. Sense 6, it's up to you, is one of the most frequent uses in speech and is invisible to learners who only know sense 1.
entries.see also: close to, ahead of, short of, as far as, inside of, depending on, to

entries.meaning: Names the event or condition whose consequence the main clause reports. It is the causal preposition of reports and investigations, where the point is usually to establish a chain rather than simply assign a reason.
examples: Two hundred jobs were lost as a result of the merger.
As a result of the audit, three policies were rewritten.
She missed a month of school as a result of the surgery.
Premiums rose sharply as a result of last year's claims.
As a result of being understaffed, the clinic cut its weekend hours.
The bridge was closed as a result of damage found during a routine inspection.
entries.русский: в результате, вследствие — событие, чьё последствие излагает главное предложение
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (as a result of being understaffed), or a nominal wh-clause (as a result of what the audit turned up). Never a that-clause — the clause-taking form is as a result of the fact that, which is worth avoiding, or simply because.
entries.pattern: [clause] as a result of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · As a result of [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: The bare adverbial as a result is not this preposition. With no complement it is a conjunctive adverb joining two sentences: Sales fell. As a result, we cut hours. The preposition requires an object. Against because of, this is heavier and frames the object as a cause whose consequences are being traced; against due to, it is adverbial and therefore never disputed.
entries.see also: because of, due to, owing to, on account of, in the wake of, thanks to

examples: We drove as far as Santa Fe and then turned around.
The trail runs as far as the second ridge.
Fires were reported as far as forty miles from the coast.
The company will go as far as a partial refund and no further.
As far as the schedule is concerned, nothing has changed.
As far as the money goes, we're covered through March.
As far as I know, the meeting is still on.

senses.head: To the point of; up to (distance)
body: We drove as far as Santa Fe and turned around.

senses.head: To the extent or limit of (degree)
body: The offer goes as far as free replacement, but no further.

senses.head: On the subject of (topic; requires is concerned or goes)
body: As far as the schedule is concerned, nothing has changed.
examples: We drove as far as Santa Fe and then turned around.
The trail runs as far as the second ridge.
Fires were reported as far as forty miles from the coast.
The company will go as far as a partial refund and no further.

As far as I know, the meeting is still on.

entries.русский: до (места); в той мере, в какой; что касается — в третьем смысле нужно is concerned
entries.complement: Three different grammars. As a preposition of distance it takes a noun phrase naming a place or point (as far as Denver). As a topic marker it takes a noun phrase that must be closed by is concerned, goes, or a similar verb — as far as the budget is concerned. As a conjunction it takes a full finite clause (as far as I know). It never takes a gerund.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] as far as [place] · As far as [noun phrase] is concerned, [clause]. · as far as [clause] (conjunction)
entries.contrast: The truncation trap. In speech Americans routinely drop the completing verb — As far as money, we're fine — and editors routinely restore it. The phrase that needs no verb is as for: As for money, we're fine is correct as it stands. The two are one syllable apart and are constantly swapped. The distance sense is treated with the movement prepositions and the full topic formula with the topic prepositions; both are linked below.
entries.see also: as for, as to, up to, short of, as far as, as far as X is concerned

entries.meaning: Shifts the topic to one item already in play, usually to say something different about it from what was just said about the others. The characteristic rhythm is a list followed by an exception: everyone else did X; as for him, he did Y.
examples: As for me, I'd rather stay home.
The others left at six. As for Dana, nobody knows.
As for the money, we'll figure that out later.
As for your second question, I don't have an answer yet.
As for finding a replacement, the search starts Monday.
He's furious. As for the rest of us, we're just tired.
entries.русский: что касается — переключает тему на один из уже названных пунктов
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (as for me, never as for I), gerund (as for finding a replacement), or a nominal wh-clause (as for what happens next). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: As for [noun phrase], [clause]. — overwhelmingly sentence-initial; the postposed [clause] as for [noun phrase] is unidiomatic.
entries.contrast: As for needs no completing verb, where as far as does: As for the budget, we're fine / As far as the budget is concerned, we're fine. Against as to, which introduces an uncertainty or a question, as for introduces a contrasting participant that has already been mentioned — it presupposes prior context and cannot open a conversation cold. Against regarding, it is conversational rather than bureaucratic.
entries.see also: as to, as far as, as regards, with regard to, as for

examples: As of January 1, the parking fee increases to twelve dollars.
The new policy takes effect as of Monday morning.
She is, as of this week, the longest-serving member of the board.
As of Friday, no one had returned the call.
As of last night, forty units were still unsold.
The balance as of the close of business was $4,318.
As of this writing, the vote count has not been certified.

senses.head: Starting from; with effect from (a future or announced point)
body: As of January 1, the fee increases.

senses.head: At the moment of; up to and including (a snapshot of a state)
body: As of last night, forty units were still unsold.
examples: As of January 1, the parking fee increases to twelve dollars.
The new policy takes effect as of Monday morning.
She is, as of this week, the longest-serving member of the board.

As of last night, forty units were still unsold.

As of this writing, the vote count has not been certified.

entries.русский: с (такого-то числа), начиная с; тж. по состоянию на (момент)
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in business, legal, and news writing
entries.complement: a time expression only — a date, a clock time, or a temporal noun (as of Monday, as of noon, as of today, as of this writing). Never a clause of any kind, never a gerund, and never a non-temporal noun: as of the merger is wrong unless the merger is being treated as a dated event.
entries.pattern: As of [time], [clause]. · [clause] as of [time].
entries.contrast: Two readings, and the tense of the main verb decides which. A present or future verb gives "starting from": As of Monday, the rate goes up. A past or perfect verb gives "at the point of, and up to": As of Friday, no one had called. Against plain from, as of fixes an official effective moment rather than a starting edge; against by, it names a snapshot rather than a deadline. British as from is rare in American English.
entries.see also: prior to, subsequent to, up to, as of, effective, from

entries.meaning: Marks the alternative that is being ruled out. Because its job is to head off a misreading, it is at its most useful when the two options are genuinely confusable.
examples: This is a recommendation, as opposed to an order.
She works in public health, as opposed to clinical medicine.
We're talking about the 1980 election, as opposed to the primary.
The grant funds research, as opposed to construction.
He chose to negotiate, as opposed to walking away.
The figure is annual, as opposed to monthly.
entries.русский: в противоположность, а не — отсекает вариант, который могли бы понять неверно
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (as opposed to waiting), or a nominal wh-clause (as opposed to what most people assume). Never a that-clause and — the to being a preposition — never a bare infinitive: as opposed to wait is wrong. The complement must be grammatically parallel to the item it corrects.
entries.pattern: [X] as opposed to [Y] · [clause], as opposed to [noun phrase / verb-ing].
entries.contrast: It does not merely contrast, it corrects — it names the thing that is not the case, usually because a reader might have assumed it was. Against instead of, which reports a substitution that actually took place (We took the train instead of driving), as opposed to draws a definitional line (a commuter train, as opposed to a freight line). Against rather than, it is heavier and more explicitly clarifying; against unlike, it does not compare qualities.
entries.see also: instead of, rather than, opposed to, in contrast to, contrary to, other than

entries.meaning: Cites an instruction, agreement, or standard as the authority for what was done. It is boilerplate — the language of purchase orders and shipping notices — and it signals institutional register more than it carries meaning.
examples: The goods were shipped as per your instructions.
Payment is due in thirty days as per the contract.
As per the attached schedule, the site closes at four.
Invoices will be processed as per company policy.
He was late again, as per usual.
The panels were installed as per the manufacturer's drawings.
entries.русский: согласно, в соответствии с — канц.; бланковый оборот заказов и накладных
entries.register: commercial and bureaucratic; widely disliked in edited prose
entries.complement: noun phrase only. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] as per [noun phrase]. · As per [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A redundancy. Latin per already means "according to," so the as adds nothing: per your request and according to your request both say what as per your request says, in fewer words. Usage guides across the board recommend per, according to, in accordance with, or following. The one form with a life of its own is the jocular fixed phrase as per usual, which nobody intends seriously.
entries.see also: according to, in accordance with, pursuant to, further to

entries.meaning: Introduces the topic of the statement. It is the most formal of the topic markers and reads as slightly archaic in American prose, where regarding, on, or about almost always fits better.
examples: As regards the second contract, negotiations are ongoing.
The report is silent as regards enforcement.
As regards staffing, the department has made no decision.
Nothing has changed as regards eligibility.
As regards funding the expansion, the board remains divided.
entries.русский: что касается, относительно — офиц., слегка архаично; без to (не as regards to)
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (as regards what was agreed). Never a that-clause. And note what cannot follow it at all: as regards to is an error — the phrase takes no to.
entries.pattern: As regards [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] as regards [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: With regard to needs its to; as regards refuses one. The reason is grammatical history: in with regard to, regard is a noun that requires the preposition to, while in as regards the -s is the third-person verb ending of an old impersonal clause ("as [it] regards"), and a verb takes its object directly. Learners who know one form contaminate the other, producing as regards to and with regards to, both wrong.
entries.see also: with regard to, as to, as for, in relation to, as regards, regarding

entries.meaning: Attaches a topic or a specification to what precedes it. Its survival in American English is almost entirely a legal phenomenon; in ordinary prose about, on, or of replaces it without loss.
examples: As to the second charge, the defense concedes nothing.
As to your fee, we can discuss it after the hearing.
There is real doubt as to whether the signature is genuine.
The parties disagree as to the meaning of Section 4.
She gave no hint as to what she would decide.
The statute is silent as to remedies.
Opinions differ sharply as to how the money should be spent.

senses.head: On the subject of (fronted topic-shifter)
body: As to the second charge, the defense concedes nothing.

senses.head: Introducing the content of a question, doubt, or dispute
body: There is real doubt as to whether the signature is genuine.
examples: As to the second charge, the defense concedes nothing.
As to your fee, we can discuss it after the hearing.
There is real doubt as to whether the signature is genuine.
The parties disagree as to the meaning of Section 4.
She gave no hint as to what she would decide.
The statute is silent as to remedies.
Opinions differ sharply as to how the money should be spent.

entries.русский: относительно, что касается; тж. вводит содержание вопроса или сомнения — юр.
entries.register: formal; very heavy in legal writing
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (as to whether the signature is genuine, as to what happened next). Never a that-clause — as to that he was late is impossible.
entries.pattern: As to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [noun of uncertainty] as to [wh-clause] · [clause] as to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Two jobs with different fates. Fronted, it is a topic-shifter and a stiffer twin of as for. Mid-sentence after a noun of uncertainty — question, doubt, dispute, evidence, confusion — it introduces the content of that uncertainty, and there it is very often deletable: no question as to whether he signed is simply no question whether he signed. Against about, it is the formal register's choice and is usually padding outside legal drafting.
entries.see also: as for, as regards, with respect to, with regard to, in relation to, as to

entries.meaning: Adds a second item while keeping it grammatically and rhetorically subordinate to the first. That subordination is the whole point, and it is why writers who mean plain coordination should use and.
examples: The fee covers materials as well as labor.
The senator, as well as two aides, was subpoenaed.
She runs the department as well as teaching two sections a semester.
He speaks Korean as well as Japanese.
As well as the main gallery, there's a sculpture garden out back.
The storm knocked out power in three counties as well as half of the next state.
She sings as well as her sister does, which is saying something.
entries.русский: а также, равно как и — второй пункт подчинён первому; сказуемое согласуется с первым
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (as well as what the grant covers). Never a that-clause. When the added item is a verb and the main clause already has a finite verb of its own, the gerund is obligatory: She runs the department as well as teaching two sections, not as well as teach. (The pattern He writes as well as directs, with two finite verbs sharing one subject, is as well as working as a coordinating conjunction, not as this preposition.)
entries.pattern: [subject], as well as [noun phrase], [singular verb] · [clause] as well as [noun phrase / verb-ing].
entries.contrast: Two traps, both common. First, verb agreement: as well as does not build a compound subject, so The manager, as well as two clerks, was present — singular, where and would give were. The same holds for along with, together with, and in addition to. Second, it is not a synonym for and: it subordinates, presenting the material after it as the lesser or already-known item, so He plays guitar as well as piano foregrounds the guitar. Distinguish also the ordinary comparative as well as meaning "as skillfully as": She sings as well as her sister is a comparison of ability, not an addition.
entries.see also: in addition to, along with, together with, on top of, as well as, besides

entries.meaning: Adds a second participant to whatever the subject is doing or undergoing. It is the neutral, everyday member of the addition group, less formal than together with and less rhetorically loaded than as well as.
examples: She arrived along with the rest of the delegation.
Send the signed form along with two forms of ID.
The coach, along with two assistants, was placed on leave.
Three warehouses burned, along with everything inside them.
Along with paying the fine, he lost his license for a year.
Her name appeared on the list along with forty others.

senses.head: In the company of; accompanying
body: She arrived along with the rest of the delegation.

senses.head: In addition to; at the same time as
body: The bill raises fees along with penalties.
examples: She arrived along with the rest of the delegation.
Send the signed form along with two forms of ID.
The coach, along with two assistants, was placed on leave.
Three warehouses burned, along with everything inside them.
Along with paying the fine, he lost his license for a year.
Her name appeared on the list along with forty others.

entries.русский: вместе с, в сопровождении; тж. наряду с — подлежащее остаётся в единственном числе
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund (along with paying the fine), or a nominal wh-clause (along with whatever else you need). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [subject], along with [noun phrase], [singular verb] · [clause] along with [noun phrase]. · Along with [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: Verb agreement trap, identical to as well as, together with, and in addition to: The coach, along with two players, was fined. The parenthetical material never joins the subject. Against plain with, along with stresses that the two share the action or the fate rather than merely being present together. Bare along is a different word — an adverb (Bring the kids along) or a preposition of path (a walk along the river).
entries.see also: together with, as well as, in addition to, along with, with

entries.meaning: Reports that two things are inconsistent with each other. The subject and the complement are treated as equals, which is why the phrase can be reversed without changing what it claims.
examples: His account is sharply at odds with the security footage.
The policy is at odds with everything the mayor campaigned on.
She has been at odds with her own caucus since January.
The findings are at odds with three earlier studies.
The new wing is wildly at odds with the rest of the block.
Their numbers are at odds with what the state reported for the same month.
entries.pronunciation note: at reduces to /ət/ · at ODZ with
entries.русский: в противоречии с, не в ладах с — о взаимной несовместимости двух вещей
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a free relative (at odds with what the data show). Never a that-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: be at odds with [noun phrase] · [noun] at odds with [noun phrase] · sharply/fundamentally/wildly at odds with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The negative counterpart of in keeping with and in line with: those report that two things fit, this reports that they do not. It stops well short of in violation of — being at odds with something alleges inconsistency, not breach — which is why it is the safe word for a claim that clashes with the evidence rather than with a rule. With a person as the object it means an ongoing quarrel (at odds with her own caucus), and there both sides are animate and the relation is mutual. Bare at odds, with no complement, is a predicate phrase and takes no object: The two of them have been at odds for years. The odds here is invariable and has nothing to do with betting.
entries.see also: in keeping with, in line with, contrary to, in contrast to, in violation of, at odds with

entries.meaning: Introduces the one thing whose absence would have changed the outcome. Legal writing has made it a term of art: the but-for test asks whether the injury would have occurred without the defendant's act.
examples: But for the seatbelt, she would not have survived.
But for a last-minute donation, the shelter would have closed.
But for his testimony, the case would never have gone to trial.
The building would be gone but for a single preservation lawsuit.
But for the weather, we would have finished the roof on Tuesday.
But for one dissenting vote, the measure would have passed unanimously.
entries.русский: если бы не — юр. «but-for тест»: без этого действия исход был бы иным
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a that-clause and never a wh-clause — the clause equivalent is the conjunction if it had not been for the fact that, or simply if ... had not.
entries.pattern: But for [noun phrase], [main clause with would, would have, or could have]. — the counterfactual verb is not optional.
entries.contrast: It requires a conditional main clause. But for means "if it had not been for," so the sentence must state what would otherwise have happened: But for the delay, we would have made the connection. A plain indicative after it (But for the delay, we missed the connection) is wrong. Against except for, which subtracts a real exception from a real situation, but for names a cause that did operate and asks the reader to imagine it away. The but here is the old preposition meaning "except," not the conjunction.
entries.see also: except for, save for, short of, in the absence of, but for, but

entries.meaning: Names the party who will receive an item and pass it along to the person actually addressed. It is one of the few complex prepositions in daily use with a standard written abbreviation, and the abbreviation is far commoner than the words.
examples: Write to her care of her publisher; she doesn't give out an address.
The check arrived care of the union hall.
Address it to Jane Ruiz, c/o Ruiz Hardware, 114 Main Street.
Packages for interns go care of the front desk.
He spent that year homeless and got his mail care of a shelter on Ninth.
Whoever follows c/o is the intermediary, not the addressee.
entries.pronunciation note: KAIR uhv — the written abbreviation c/o is read aloud as care of, or spelled out see-oh
entries.русский: на адрес, для передачи через (кого-то) — почт., сокр. c/o
entries.register: neutral; addressing conventions, correspondence, and forms
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the intermediate recipient — a person, a business, or an institution. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [addressee], care of [noun phrase] · [addressee] c/o [noun phrase], [street address]
entries.variants: written c/o on an envelope or address line — lowercase, with the slash, no periods — and occasionally as the single character ℅. British usage is identical.
entries.contrast: The complement is the intermediary, never the addressee: Jane Ruiz, c/o Ruiz Hardware means the letter is for Jane and the store will hand it to her. Reversing the two is the standard error and delivers the letter to the wrong name. Against Attn:, which routes mail inside an organization that is itself the addressee, care of routes mail through a party who is not the addressee at all. Against courtesy of, which credits a source and merely sounds similar, it has nothing in common but the first word.
entries.see also: courtesy of, for the account of, on behalf of, by way of, to

entries.meaning: Makes the main clause conditional on a factor that may vary. It is the standard way English states a range of outcomes without writing a conditional sentence.
examples: The trip takes two or three hours, depending on traffic.
Depending on the weather, the ceremony will be inside or out.
Fees range from $40 to $120 depending on the size of the lot.
Depending on what the inspector finds, we may have to start over.
She'll fly or drive, depending on whether the fare drops.
Turnout could double or halve depending on how the case is decided.
entries.русский: в зависимости от — ставит главное предложение в зависимость от переменного фактора
entries.complement: noun phrase or a nominal wh-clause — depending on what you order, depending on whether it rains, depending on how far you drive. Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause], depending on [noun phrase / wh-clause]. · Depending on [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.variants: depending upon is the formal variant and means exactly the same thing.
entries.contrast: It has frozen completely: it needs no subject and cannot dangle, unlike the live participle in Depending on his brother for rides, he never bought a car, where depending still belongs to he. Against according to, which reports what a source says, depending on names a variable that determines the outcome. Its free acceptance of wh-clauses puts it in a very small group with regardless of, irrespective of, and as to.
entries.see also: according to, regardless of, in the event of, on the basis of, considering

examples: Except for two typos, the manuscript is clean.
The office is empty except for the night guard.
I like everything on the menu except for the oysters.
Except for Tuesday, I'm free all week.
Except for the rain, we would have finished the roof.
The team would be in first place except for a bad October.

senses.head: Apart from; with the exception of
body: Except for two typos, the manuscript is clean.

senses.head: If it were not for (a factor that prevented something)
body: Except for the rain, we would have finished the roof.
examples: Except for two typos, the manuscript is clean.
The office is empty except for the night guard.
I like everything on the menu except for the oysters.
Except for Tuesday, I'm free all week.
Except for the rain, we would have finished the roof.
The team would be in first place except for a bad October.

entries.русский: кроме, за исключением; тж. если бы не (помеха, которая всё сорвала)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (except for me), gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (except for what he told the police). Never a that-clause — the clause form is the conjunction except that (The house is perfect except that it has no garage).
entries.pattern: Except for [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] except for [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Except for versus bare except. Use except for when the exception is fronted (Except for Tuesday, I'm free) and when it subtracts from a whole rather than from a matching list item; use bare except when the exception is parallel to something explicit in the sentence (Everyone came except Dave). Against apart from and aside from, which can also mean "in addition to," except for only subtracts — which makes it the right choice whenever the exception reading must be unmistakable.
entries.see also: with the exception of, apart from, aside from, save for, but for, other than, except for

entries.meaning: Marks the person signing as an agent acting for the named principal. It appears above a signature line far more often than inside a sentence.
examples: Signed for and on behalf of Ardmore Holdings, LLC.
The attorney-in-fact executed the deed for and on behalf of her father.
Counsel appeared for and on behalf of all four defendants.
The treasurer accepted the award for and on behalf of the association.
He signs for and on behalf of the partnership, not in his own name.
Every plain-language guide says to cut the for and; the form books keep it anyway.
entries.русский: за и от имени — юр.; формула над подписью представителя принципала
entries.register: formal; signature blocks, powers of attorney, and corporate resolutions
entries.type: complex (a doublet — two coordinated prepositional frames, one object)
entries.complement: a single noun phrase naming the principal. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: Signed for and on behalf of [noun phrase] · [agent], for and on behalf of [principal]
entries.contrast: Unlike by or on behalf of, which closes a real gap, this one is padding. On behalf of alone carries the entire meaning, and the added for is one of the many legal doublets — give and grant, null and void, save and except — left over from the centuries when English drafters paired an English word with a French or Latin one. Every plain-language drafting manual says to cut it; it survives because signature blocks get copied rather than written. Note that the traditional distinction between on behalf of (as agent) and in behalf of (for the benefit of) still governs the on behalf of half of it.
entries.see also: on behalf of, by or on behalf of, in behalf of, in and for, in the name of, by and through

entries.meaning: Names the outcome whose prospect stopped the subject from acting. The phrase reports a motive rather than a cause, and the motive is always avoidance.
examples: She said nothing for fear of making it worse.
Nobody reported the leak for fear of losing the contract.
Witnesses would not come forward for fear of retaliation.
They moved the horses inside for fear of the storm.
He avoided the subject entirely for fear of another argument.
The family kept the diagnosis quiet for fear of what the neighbors would say.
entries.русский: из страха перед, боясь — мотив избегания, удержавший от действия
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (for fear of waking the baby). Never a that-clause — the clause-taking companion is the conjunction for fear that (for fear that the baby would wake), which is a different item, exactly as in case is to in case of. A free relative is fine, since it is a noun phrase (for fear of what the neighbors would say), and never an infinitive: for fear of to wake the baby is wrong.
entries.pattern: [negative or cautious clause] for fear of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · [clause] for fear that [clause] — the conjunction, not this preposition.
entries.variants: out of fear of is the looser, more psychological variant. Do not confuse it with in fear of, which means "afraid of" and names a state rather than a motive: living in fear of deportation is how someone feels, he said nothing for fear of deportation is why he acted.
entries.contrast: It gives the feared outcome as the reason something was not done, so the main clause is characteristically negative, hedged, or evasive — said nothing, never reported it, kept the door locked. Against because of, the feared thing need never have happened at all, which is exactly the difference between a cause and a motive. Against to avoid, which takes the same gerund and names the same purpose, for fear of adds the emotion and concedes the timidity. Its structural neighbor is for lack of, which blames an absence where this one blames an anticipation.
entries.see also: for lack of, because of, in case of, on account of, for fear of

entries.meaning: Gives the missing thing as the reason for the outcome, and the outcome is nearly always a failure, a refusal, or a collapse. Because the phrase blames an absence, it cannot take an object that was present.
examples: The case was dismissed for lack of evidence.
The project died for lack of funding.
For lack of a better word, the meeting was a disaster.
Two positions went unfilled for lack of qualified applicants.
The garden failed for lack of water, not for lack of attention.
entries.русский: за неимением, из-за отсутствия — нехватка как причина провала или отказа
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically a bare abstract or mass noun (for lack of evidence, for lack of funding). Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] for lack of [noun phrase]. · for lack of anything better · for lack of a better [noun]
entries.variants: For want of is the older and more literary twin — For want of a nail the shoe was lost — and is somewhat commoner in British English; for lack of is the ordinary American form. Both take the same complement, and neither puts an article on the noun unless the noun demands one.
entries.contrast: It states a cause that consists in an absence, which is exactly what separates it from because of: dismissed because of the evidence and dismissed for lack of evidence say opposite things. Against in the absence of, which supplies a condition and looks forward (in the absence of an agreement, state law governs), for lack of supplies a reason and looks back at something that has already failed. The apologetic formula for lack of a better word is fixed and cannot be varied.
entries.see also: in the absence of, because of, short of, devoid of, for lack of, for want of

entries.meaning: Assigns the financial consequences of a transaction to a named party. It is the phrase that tells you whose money is moving, which in trade finance is very nearly the only question there is.
examples: The bank issued the credit for the account of the importer.
Shares were purchased for the account of three separate clients.
Storage charges are for the account of the consignee.
Freight and insurance are for account of the buyer under these terms.
The wire was sent for the account of the escrow, not the seller.
On behalf of names who is represented; for the account of names who pays.
entries.русский: за счёт (такого-то) — фин.; чьи деньги задействованы в сделке
entries.register: formal; banking, trade finance, brokerage, and shipping documents
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the party whose account is charged or credited. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [payment or purchase] for the account of [noun phrase] · for account of [noun phrase] (article-less, in trade documents) · for the account and risk of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The complement is whoever bears the cost, who is often not the party performing the act — a broker buys for the account of a client, and a bank pays a letter of credit for the account of the applicant. Against on behalf of, which names who is represented, this one names who pays; the two usually pick out the same party but do not have to. Against care of, which routes a delivery, it routes a charge. The shipping formula for account and risk of adds who bears the loss as well as the cost.
entries.see also: on behalf of, to the order of, in trust for, care of, at the expense of

entries.meaning: States the aim an action was designed to serve. Its survival is entirely institutional: it marks the purpose as officially declared rather than merely intended.
examples: The land was acquired for the purpose of building a transfer station.
The account exists for the purpose of holding client funds and nothing else.
For the purposes of this section, "resident" means a person domiciled in the state.
Records may be retained for the purpose of audit.
He formed the company for the purpose of limiting his personal liability.
entries.русский: с целью, в целях — офиц.; цель объявлена, а не просто подразумевается
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund only (for the purpose of raising revenue). Because of is a preposition, for the purpose of to raise revenue is wrong, and so is for the purpose to raise revenue. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] for the purpose of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · For the purposes of [this section], [definition].
entries.variants: The plural for the purposes of is the standard opening of a definition clause — For the purposes of this Act, "employee" means… — and is not interchangeable with the singular, which states an aim rather than a scope.
entries.contrast: Against the plain infinitive of purpose, which says the same thing in two words, this is nearly always padding: for the purpose of reducing costs is to reduce costs. Keep it where the purpose has to appear as a formal element — tax law, permits, definitions — and cut it everywhere else. Against with a view to, which takes the same gerund but implies the goal has not been reached, for the purpose of simply names the aim; against for the sake of, which names a beneficiary or a value, this names an objective.
entries.see also: with a view to, for the sake of, in the interest of, for the purpose of, in order to

entries.meaning: Names the person served or the end pursued. The purpose reading is the commoner one in writing, where it introduces a stylistic or argumentative goal rather than a beneficiary.
examples: They stayed together for the sake of the children.
She took the fall for the sake of the team.
He gave up the appeal for the sake of his mother, who could not face another hearing.
For the sake of clarity, let me restate the question.
He conceded the point for the sake of argument.
For the sake of keeping the peace, nobody mentioned the will.
Don't argue for the sake of arguing.

senses.head: For the benefit of (a person or group)
body: They stayed together for the sake of the children.

senses.head: In order to achieve or preserve (a purpose or quality)
body: For the sake of clarity, let me restate the question.
examples: They stayed together for the sake of the children.
She took the fall for the sake of the team.
He gave up the appeal for the sake of his mother, who could not face another hearing.
For the sake of clarity, let me restate the question.
He conceded the point for the sake of argument.
For the sake of keeping the peace, nobody mentioned the will.
Don't argue for the sake of arguing.

entries.pronunciation note: casual /fər ðə ˈseɪ kə/ · for thuh SAYK uhv
entries.русский: ради (кого-то, чьего-то блага); тж. ради (ясности, краткости, порядка)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (for the sake of keeping the peace). Never a that-clause; a free relative is possible but uncommon (for the sake of whoever comes after us).
entries.pattern: [clause] for the sake of [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · For the sake of [noun phrase], [clause]. · for [possessive] sake (fixed: for heaven's sake)
entries.variants: for the sake of argument and the possessive pattern for argument's sake are both current; the possessive drops both the and of.
entries.contrast: The two senses below are told apart by whether the object is animate. Against on behalf of, which means "as the agent of," this means "for the benefit of," and confusing them makes a speaker claim authority they do not have. The possessive forms — for heaven's sake, for old times' sake, for goodness' sake — are a separate frozen construction and take no of.
entries.see also: on behalf of, with a view to, in the name of, in search of, for

entries.term: for the use and benefit of
entries.respell: weak /fər ðə ˈjus ən ˈbɛnəfə ɾə/
entries.meaning: Names the party who is to enjoy property, or the proceeds of an action, held or brought by somebody else. It is the fullest member of a family whose shorter forms are for the benefit of and in trust for.
examples: The land was conveyed to the city for the use and benefit of its residents.
Funds are held by the trustee for the use and benefit of the minor children.
The action is brought for the use and benefit of the State of Nevada.
The strip along the creek was dedicated for the use and benefit of the public.
Insurance proceeds are receivable for the use and benefit of the lienholder.
A plain-language drafter writes simply for.
entries.pronunciation note: for thuh YOOSS und BEN-uh-fit uhv
entries.русский: в пользу и на благо — юр.; полная форма for the benefit of и in trust for
entries.register: formal; trusts, deeds, public dedications, and ex rel. pleadings
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the beneficiary — a person, a class, or the public. Never a that-clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: held/conveyed/dedicated for the use and benefit of [noun phrase] · [State] ex rel. [relator], for the use and benefit of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Another legal doublet: use and benefit say substantially the same thing, and the pair descends from the medieval "use," the direct ancestor of the modern trust. It differs from in trust for only in length and setting — in trust for is the banking form, for the use and benefit of the conveyancing one. In several states a public-money or qui tam action is captioned for the use and benefit of the state, which is where a non-lawyer is likeliest to run into it. Plain-language drafters cut the whole thing to for.
entries.see also: in trust for, in behalf of, for and on behalf of, for the sake of, for the benefit of

entries.meaning: Links the present message to an earlier one. It is nearly pure register: it carries no meaning that the reader would miss if the phrase were cut.
examples: Further to your email of March 3, the position remains open.
Further to our conversation, I've attached the revised figures.
Further to the committee's request, the data is enclosed.
Further to my previous letter, the deadline has been extended.
Further to the notice of April 12, no further action is required.
entries.русский: в дополнение к, в развитие — канц.; связывает письмо с предыдущим, смысла не добавляет
entries.register: formal correspondence; markedly more British than American
entries.complement: noun phrase only — a document, a message, or a prior exchange. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause, never a gerund, and never a bare infinitive.
entries.pattern: Further to [noun phrase], [clause]. — almost always the opening words of a letter or an email.
entries.contrast: A letter-opening formula meaning "following up on." In American business writing it reads as imported; following up on, regarding, or plain about is the native equivalent. Against with reference to, which points at a document as a source, further to points at a prior exchange and promises to continue it. Do not confuse with the comparative adverb further (We went further than planned), which takes no object.
entries.see also: with reference to, as per, in response to, pursuant to, regarding

Other than a sore shoulder, he came through it fine.

You cannot reach the island other than by ferry.
He has never spoken about it other than briefly, and never on the record.

senses.head: Apart from; besides
body: We have no evidence other than his statement.

senses.head: In any way but; differently from

entries.русский: кроме, помимо; тж. иначе как (иначе как паромом туда не добраться)
entries.complement: unusually wide — a noun phrase, an objective-case pronoun (other than her), a gerund, an adverb (other than briefly), a whole prepositional phrase (other than by mail), or a nominal wh-clause (nothing other than what he said). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [negative or universal clause] other than [complement] · Other than [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: It is most idiomatic after a negative or a universal — nothing other than, anyone other than, no way other than. After a plain positive statement it sounds stiff. Against except for, it is more formal and far more willing to take adverbial complements: other than by mail is fine, except for by mail is not. Against besides, which can add a second item, other than only subtracts. Neither half is this word on its own: other is a determiner or adjective (the other door), and than by itself is the comparative — a conjunction before a clause (taller than I am) and a preposition before a pronoun (taller than me). And it is other than, never other then.
entries.see also: except for, apart from, aside from, rather than, other than, besides

entries.meaning: Adds something to a total that was already complete. The baseline has to be recoverable from the sentence, or the phrase has nothing to measure the surplus against.
examples: She receives a housing allowance over and above her salary.
The fee is charged over and above the standard shipping rate.
Over and above the fine, he lost his license for a year.
They asked for two more inspectors over and above what the budget allowed.
The volunteers put in three hundred hours over and above running the shelter itself.
entries.русский: сверх, помимо — прибавка к итогу, который уже был полным
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (over and above meeting the minimum). Never a that-clause; a free relative is fine (over and above what the contract requires).
entries.pattern: [clause] over and above [noun phrase]. · Over and above [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A four-word in addition to with one extra claim: that what came before was already enough. Over and above her salary presents the salary as the expected part and the rest as surplus, where in addition to her salary is neutral about sufficiency. Against besides, it is heavier and more emphatic. Neither half carries the meaning alone — over and above are ordinary spatial prepositions elsewhere, and the frozen pair is not spatial at all; nor can the two words be separated. The similar-sounding above and beyond is a different fixed phrase and describes effort rather than amount.
entries.see also: in addition to, as well as, on top of, together with, over and above

entries.русский: а не; вместо — предпочтение одному варианту перед другим
entries.complement: the freest complement in this file. A noun phrase (rather than the bus), a gerund (rather than complaining), a bare infinitive (rather than complain), an adjective (structural rather than personal), an adverb, a prepositional phrase, or a nominal wh-clause (rather than what was proposed). Never a that-clause. After a to-infinitive it takes a bare infinitive: He chose to walk rather than wait.
entries.pattern: [X] rather than [Y] — X and Y parallel · Rather than [Y], [clause]. · [subject], rather than [noun phrase], [singular verb]
entries.contrast: The bare-infinitive privilege is what separates it from instead of, which must nominalize: rather than complain is correct, instead of complain is not. Verb agreement follows the as well as rule: The manager, rather than the clerks, is responsible. Note also that rather than is often a conjunction rather than a preposition — the test is what it joins: parallel phrases make it a preposition, full clauses make it a conjunction.
entries.see also: instead of, as opposed to, in place of, in lieu of, other than

entries.meaning: Removes one item from an otherwise complete picture. Its natural home is descriptive narrative, where the exception is meant to stand out against an emptiness or a uniformity.
examples: The street was silent save for a dog barking two blocks over.
The house was untouched save for a cracked window at the back.
Save for one abstention, the vote was unanimous.
He remembered nothing of the evening save for the drive home.
Every ship in the harbor was lost, save for the two in dry dock.
Save for an hour on Sunday, she worked the entire week.
entries.русский: кроме, за исключением — книжн.; исключение на фоне пустоты или однообразия
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (save for what little was left). Never a that-clause — the clause-taking form is the conjunction save that.
entries.pattern: [clause], save for [noun phrase]. · Save for [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.variants: bare save (The room was empty save one chair) is older and even more literary; saving is archaic; save that is the clause-taking conjunction.
entries.contrast: A consciously elevated except for. In American prose it reads as a deliberate stylistic choice rather than a neutral one, and using it in ordinary business writing draws attention to itself. Against but for, which is counterfactual and demands a conditional main clause, save for simply subtracts from a real situation. Do not confuse the preposition with the verb save; the preposition never has a subject of its own.
entries.see also: except for, but for, with the exception of, apart from, save for, save

entries.meaning: Offers one or more members of a class as illustrations of it. The class must be stated first, which is why such as cannot open a sentence the way like sometimes can.
examples: Root vegetables such as carrots and parsnips keep for months.
Heavy industries such as steel and shipbuilding left the region entirely.
She avoids stimulants such as coffee and black tea.
The grant covers direct costs such as travel, equipment, and printing.
Small tasks such as returning calls pile up fast.
Cities such as Tucson and Phoenix face the same water problem.
entries.русский: такие как, например — примеры из класса, который назван до этого
entries.complement: noun phrase (usually a list) or gerund. Never a that-clause, never a wh-clause. The complement must be a genuine member of the class named before it — fruits such as apples, not fruits such as sweetness.
entries.pattern: [general noun] such as [example], [example] · [clause], such as [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Such as introduces examples; like introduces resemblances. The traditional rule reserves like for comparison and such as for exemplification: a writer like Hemingway means someone who resembles him, a writer such as Hemingway means him, offered as an instance. Speech ignores the distinction; edited prose still keeps it. Note the related split in the same pair: ✗ as a preposition like takes a noun phrase (He works like a machine), while as introduces a role (He works as a machine operator) and, as a conjunction, a full clause (Do as I say) — like I say is spoken English that edited prose still changes to as I say. Two mechanical points on such as: no comma before it when the examples restrict the class (fruits such as apples and pears), a comma when they merely illustrate; and ✗ do not end the list with etc., since such as already announces that the list is partial. Neither half stands alone: bare such is a determiner (such a mess) and bare as is a different preposition or a conjunction; only the pair is this item.
entries.see also: as opposed to, in the way of, including, as, like

entries.meaning: Attaches supplementary material to a subject without merging the two. Its usefulness in drafting comes precisely from that refusal to merge: the primary item stays primary.
examples: The application, together with the filing fee, must reach the office by Friday.
The deed was recorded together with two easements.
Together with her brother, she inherited the farm.
The report, together with all supporting exhibits, was filed Monday.
Send the transcript together with three letters of recommendation.
The principal, together with accrued interest, comes to just over $9,000.
She arrived together with two lawyers and said almost nothing.

senses.head: In the company of; accompanied by
body: Together with her brother, she inherited the farm.

senses.head: In addition to (adding an item without joining it to the subject)
body: The application, together with the filing fee, must reach the office by Friday.

entries.русский: вместе с, в сопровождении; тж. в дополнение к — сказуемое остаётся в единственном числе
entries.register: formal to neutral; common in drafting and in formal reports
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a nominal wh-clause (together with whatever documents you have). Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [subject], together with [noun phrase], [singular verb] · [clause], together with [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Verb agreement trap, the same one as along with, as well as, and in addition to: the added item is parenthetical, so the verb agrees with the original subject alone — The report, together with the appendices, was filed Monday. Against along with, it is the more formal of the two and the one that appears in contracts and filings; against and, it deliberately refuses to build a compound subject. Bare together is an adverb and takes no object: We went together.
entries.see also: along with, as well as, in addition to, in conjunction with, together with, with

entries.pronunciation note: weak /əp əˈɡɛn(t)s/ — up reduces to /əp/ and the final t routinely drops · up uh-GENST
entries.русский: вплотную к, прислонив к; перед лицом (препятствия); up against it — в большой беде
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; never a gerund and never a that-clause. A free relative is idiomatic in sense 2 (up against whatever the league can put on the field). In the fixed idiom up against it the complement is the invariable pronoun it and nothing else may replace it.
entries.pattern: be up against [noun phrase] · [clause] up against [noun phrase] · be up against it (fixed)
entries.contrast: Sense 1 is not really a unit at all — it is the adverb up plus the ordinary preposition against, and you can drop the up (the ladder against the wall). Sense 2 is the frozen idiom, and there the up cannot go: We're up against a deadline is not We're against a deadline. Against facing, sense 2 always implies difficulty and usually implies an unfair contest.
entries.see also: in the face of, ahead of, close to, short of, against

entries.meaning: Either offers a person's willingness or announces that something is on the block. The two senses never collide in practice, because the subject settles which one you are hearing.
examples: Is anybody up for a swim before dinner?
She's up for anything as long as it isn't a nine a.m. meeting.
Three of the five council seats are up for election in November.
The lease is up for renewal at the end of the quarter.
The house went up for auction after the second missed payment.
He's up for partner this year and pretending not to think about it.

senses.head: (of a person) Willing to do or take part in
body: Is anybody up for a swim?

senses.head: (of a thing) Due to be decided, offered, or considered
body: Three of the five seats are up for election.
examples: Is anybody up for a swim before dinner?
