entries.pronunciation note: both words reduce, giving uhp-fer · UP for
entries.русский: не прочь, готовый (на что-то); выставленный на (выборы, продажу, рассмотрение)
entries.register: informal to neutral; conversation, politics, sports, and workplace talk
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (up for going out), and the gerund is normal in sense 1. Never a that-clause and never a bare infinitive: up for go out is wrong.
entries.pattern: be up for [noun phrase / verb-ing] · be up for [election / review / renewal / auction] · Anyone up for [noun phrase]?
entries.contrast: Two live senses, told apart entirely by the subject. With a person as subject it means "willing" (I'm up for a walk); with a thing as subject it means "due to be decided" (the contract is up for renewal). Against in line for, sense 2 says only that a decision is coming, not that the subject will get anything — a senator up for reelection may well lose. Against up to, a different phrase altogether (up to no good, up to you), and against up against, which means confronted by, this one is about willingness and candidacy. Bare up is an adverb and takes no object.
entries.see also: up against, up to, in line for, in the mood for, in the market for

entries.meaning: Marks the far end of a range and states explicitly that the endpoint falls inside it. It is one of the very few multi-word legalisms that plain-language editors leave alone, because the shorter form loses information.
examples: Violations may result in discipline up to and including termination.
Claims filed up to and including December 31 are covered under the old policy.
The permit covers loads up to and including four tons.
Every level of management up to and including the chief executive was briefed.
Chapters one up to and including six are on the midterm.
Where the endpoint has to be excluded, write up to but not including.
entries.русский: вплоть до включительно — юр.; прямо оговаривает, что крайняя точка входит в диапазон
entries.register: formal to neutral; policies, statutes, employee handbooks, and specifications
entries.type: complex (an ordinary preposition coordinated with a participial one, sharing a single object)
entries.complement: noun phrase naming an endpoint — a date, a quantity, a level, a sanction. Never a that-clause, and no gerund in this frame, although including on its own takes one elsewhere.
entries.pattern: [range] up to and including [endpoint] · discipline up to and including termination (fixed collocation)
entries.contrast: The phrase exists to settle a genuine ambiguity, which is what separates it from the ornamental doublets in this file. Bare up to is really unclear about its endpoint — up to ten copies may or may not include the tenth — and up to and including removes the doubt. The opposite fix is up to but not including, or the pair inclusive and exclusive. In American employment writing the phrase has one famous home: disciplinary action up to and including termination, which is the standard formula for "we can fire you for this."
entries.see also: up to, in excess of, short of, including, inclusive of

entries.meaning: States that something was accomplished without falling back on an available remedy or resource. The tone is usually approving: the point is that the harder or costlier option turned out not to be needed.
examples: The dispute was settled without recourse to litigation.
They balanced the budget without recourse to the rainy-day fund.
Can the passage be read without recourse to the commentary?
The clinic operated for two years without recourse to borrowing.
Without recourse to federal aid, the county rebuilt both bridges itself.
On a check endorsement, bare without recourse means something else entirely.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /wəˈðaʊt ˈrikɔrs tə/ · with-OWT REE-korss too
entries.русский: не прибегая к — обошлись без имевшегося запасного средства, обычно одобрительно
entries.register: formal; policy writing and scholarship, and — in the bare form without recourse — banking law
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (without recourse to borrowing). Because this to is a preposition, without recourse to borrow is wrong. Never a that-clause. A free relative is fine (without recourse to what the older statute allowed).
entries.pattern: [clause] without recourse to [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · Without recourse to [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: It means "without falling back on," so the object is a resource, remedy, or last resort — the courts, force, the reserves, the commentary. Against plain without, it adds that the unused thing was available and would have been the obvious fallback. Bare without recourse is a different, technical item: endorsed on a negotiable instrument it means the endorser disclaims liability if the paper is not paid, and there it takes no object at all. Against without regard to, which means "leaving out of account," this one means "not resorting to," and the two are not interchangeable.
entries.see also: without regard to, in the absence of, short of, failing, without

entries.meaning: States that the thing named was left out of the reckoning. Whether it cuts toward fairness or toward recklessness depends entirely on whether the ignored thing ought to have mattered.
examples: Applicants are considered without regard to race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.
Benefits are calculated without regard to the employee's length of service.
The agreement is governed by New York law, without regard to its conflict-of-laws principles.
He kept spending without regard to what any of it was doing to the reserves.
Without regard to cost, the safest design would have used two pumps.
The last word is to: without regard of is not English.
entries.русский: без учёта, невзирая на — названное не принималось в расчёт
entries.register: formal; statutes, contracts, and policy language
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (without regard to being asked), or a nominal wh-clause (without regard to what it costs). Because the to is prepositional, without regard to be asked is wrong. Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] without regard to [noun phrase / verb-ing]. · Without regard to [noun phrase], [clause]. · without regard to its conflict-of-laws principles (fixed, in choice-of-law clauses)
entries.variants: without regard for occurs and is somewhat commoner in the "disregarding someone's interests" sense (without regard for her feelings); the legal collocations all take to.
entries.contrast: The neutral, formal twin of regardless of and irrespective of, and unlike either of them it is at home in a statute. The last word is to, not of: without regard of is an error. Against without recourse to, which means "not falling back on," this means "not taking into account." Two opposite tones share the phrase: nondiscrimination language uses it approvingly (without regard to race, color, or national origin), and criticism uses it accusingly (without regard to the consequences).
entries.see also: regardless of, irrespective of, without recourse to, in spite of, notwithstanding
